governance_posts.title: Risk Stewards: Supply and Borrow Cap Increases on Aave V3 / 2026.11.08
governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

Aave V3 Core:

  • Increase borrow cap for USDC from 2,600,000,000 to 2,750,000,000.
  • Increase supply cap for USDe from 550,000,000 to 750,000,000.

USDC (Aave V3 Core)

USDC has reached 99.0% borrow cap utilization (2.57B / 2.6B) on the Aave V3 Core instance.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 8, 2026

The top 20 USDC borrowers run health factors between 1.02 and 3.07 with a median of 1.76, and the largest borrower accounts for about 14% of outstanding debt. Collateral behind these positions is mainly ETH and BTC assets, with 5 of the 20 posting WETH, 5 weETH, 4 wstETH, 4 cbBTC, and 3 WBTC, alongside 3 posting USDe and 3 sUSDe, so HF in the cohort tracks the ETH and BTC prices and, on the USDe and sUSDe positions, the exchange rate of those assets against the stablecoin debt.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the borrow cap from 2.6B to 2.75B on Aave V3 Core, which places the reserve at approximately 93.6% post-change borrow cap utilization. The proposed borrow cap corresponds to 96.6% reserve utilization at current supply, above the 94% optimal point.

USDe (Aave V3 Core)

USDe has reached 100.0% supply cap utilization (550M / 550M) on the Aave V3 Core instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 8, 2026

The top 20 USDe suppliers hold about 99% of the supply, with 18 of 20 carrying debt at health factors between 1.02 and 2.30 and a median of 1.03. Supply is concentrated, with the largest supplier at about 61% and the top 5 at about 91%, and the debt is denominated almost entirely in stablecoins (USDC and USDT).

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 550M to 750M on Aave V3 Core, which places the reserve at approximately 73.3% post-change supply cap utilization.

Specification

Supply Caps

Instance Asset Current Supply Cap Recommended Supply Cap
Aave V3 Core USDe 550,000,000 750,000,000

Borrow Caps

Instance Asset Current Borrow Cap Recommended Borrow Cap
Aave V3 Core USDC 2,600,000,000 2,750,000,000

Next Steps

We will move forward and implement these updates via the Risk Steward process. The implemented changes can be reviewed on the LlamaRisk Risk Stewards Dashboard.

Disclosure

This review was independently prepared by LlamaRisk, a DeFi risk service provider funded in part by the Aave DAO. LlamaRisk is not directly affiliated with the protocol(s) reviewed in this assessment and did not receive any compensation from the protocol(s) or their affiliated entities for this work.

The information provided should not be construed as legal, financial, tax, or professional advice.

governance_posts.title: Per-Asset Liquidation Thresholds Underpredict Co-Liquidation by 301×
governance_posts.description:
Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets.

I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026).

Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution.

Results:

  • 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced.
  • 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced.
  • 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this.

All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds.

The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX).

The test takes 30 seconds and uses no API keys. The full methodology, results, and test script are at The Short Version — The Rogue Wave — sections 17 and 18.

What needs to change: The per-asset threshold model must be replaced with a joint probability model that accounts for tail correlation across collateral assets. The mathematics exists — it was developed after 2008 specifically because the same independence assumption failed in CDO pricing. Portfolio-level liquidation thresholds must tighten as correlated assets are added, not average.

This is not a code bug. The code correctly implements the specified thresholds. The thresholds themselves are structurally inadequate for the correlation that exists in the data.

I am requesting assistance with the possible recovery of 2 AAVE tokens accidentally transferred from my Revolut account directly to the official AAVE token contract on Ethereum.

Revolut 1 Call 0x4c9591ef Method on Revolut 5 | Success | Oct-28-2026 04:25:11 PM (UTC)

Revolut confirms that the withdrawal was completed. The amount transferred was 2 AAVE, excluding the withdrawal fee.

I understand that recovery is not guaranteed and that any recovery process may require technical assessment and governance approval.

I can provide my Revolut withdrawal statement and additional proof of the transaction through an appropriate verification process.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

governance_posts.title: [ARFC] Repositioning Aave V3 Core Around Established & Liquid Collateral
governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk proposes to reposition Aave V3 Core as an instance for liquid, bluechip collateral, while the broader range of asset classes is served by Aave V4, where the Risk Premium parameter granularly prices the additional risk each collateral asset carries and more flexible isolation levers exist. The proposal is the next step of the deprecation work, which wound down low-adoption reserves and instances and deprecated the price feeds of long-tail assets.

The proposal covers rsETH, osETH, LBTC, tBTC and rETH on Core, together with a group of lower-exposure reserves. As of 9 November 2026 these assets held $1.33B of collateral backing $1.03B of debt.

The initial measure is to freeze each reserve in scope, which stops new supply and sets the LTV to zero while leaving existing positions untouched and unaffected. Reserves that are frozen, or frozen by this ARFC, are borrowable, and still carry more than $20k of debt also have their reserve factor raised to 99%. We will then work with each asset issuer and with the largest borrowers on an orderly migration, and allow positions to unwind naturally before taking any further action. The proposal also approves a defined range of follow-up controls, including stepwise liquidation threshold reductions and, as the final step of the process, interest rate adjustments with targeted rebates, to be applied through Risk Stewards or Direct-to-AIP proposals only where exposure migration does not happen within the next months.

Background

The repositioning continues a sequence of steps that the DAO has approved over the past months. The Aave Risk Framework set out the criteria and review cadence against which collateral on Aave is assessed, including issuer transparency, operational resourcing and the architecture between a token and its underlying. The Low Adoption Asset Deprecation ARFC wound down 71 reserves across eleven deployments, together with six whole markets, which held about $98M of supply in total. The Oracle Deprecation ARFC replaced the price feeds of long-tail assets with fixed values ahead of their full wind-down.

The earlier rounds addressed reserves whose usage no longer justified their operational cost, and granted eBTC, BTC.b, tETH and the governance tokens a three-month exemption. governance_posts.title: [ARFC] Dynamic Caps Oracle: Rate Limiter
governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk is building Aave’s Risk Layer: automated risk solutions that make expert risk judgment verifiable, with every parameter, bound and action checkable onchain. The Aave Risk Framework set this direction in June by making continuous risk oracles part of the protocol’s standing infrastructure. Governance and manual review can trail a fast-moving event by hours, and the evolution of AI capabilities keeps shortening the time between finding a weakness and exploiting it, so protection has to run continuously and at machine speed. LlamaGuard PT went live in September as the first of these solutions. We continue the rollout with LlamaGuard Caps as the next addition.

Aave’s greatest strength is its liquidity, deep enough to move capital instantly and at scale. Defending access to that liquidity programmatically protects Aave’s users, even when a failure elsewhere in DeFi puts compromised collateral or stolen assets in play. LlamaGuard Caps hardens Aave’s perimeter. Its first stage, a borrow rate limiter for Aave V3, gives each reserve a margin of borrowing room above its debt, sized to the reserve. That room refills automatically as organic demand uses it and is cut back when large repayments open up more than the reserve needs. Everyday borrowing keeps instant access to liquidity. A large draw, though, has to wait for each refill, giving the Protocol Guardian reasonable time to respond to illegitimate activity. Integrated institutional clients and other approved large borrowers will have a dedicated pathway that meets their capital demand quickly.

LlamaGuard Caps will run on the Risk Agents stack that Aave Governance already owns. Raises are computed on Chainlink CRE, on the same oracle network that delivers the price feeds Aave relies on, and every bound is enforced onchain. Aave’s core contracts and existing agents stay unchanged, and the new smart contract surface is small. Every lever stays with Aave governance: Risk Stewards and governance continue to set each cap’s maximum, and automation controls only how fast room opens beneath it. This proposal is the first stage of a gradual rollout. Later stages will set the ceiling itself from live liquidity conditions and extend dynamic protection to supply caps, Aave V4 and cross-market modules, each calibrated on live data from the stage before.

Threat model

Two external threats have proved the most consequential for Aave.

  1. An attacker deposits maliciously obtained collateral that is worth less than the oracle reports, and borrows against it.
  2. An attacker gains control of many different assets, deposits them as collateral and borrows assets that can’t be frozen, as fast as possible.

In both cases the damage starts outside Aave, with a compromised asset or a compromised holder. Aave is affected because its deep, instant liquidity is what the attacker needs to turn that position into assets that can leave. Aave can’t prevent these events. It can control how quickly its liquidity is drawn once one is under way, and so how much time the Protocol Guardian has to investigate and respond.

Exposure under static caps

Borrow caps on Aave are set by the Risk Stewards or through governance AIPs. Each change is generated programmatically but still needs human approval, through the Risk Steward multisig or a governance vote, and must wait out a minimum delay before the next one. A cap therefore has to hold enough room for the growth expected before its next revision. That headroom is open by design. Over the year from October 2025 to October 2026, standing borrow headroom averaged 41.1% of debt on Core WETH, 75.3% on Core USDT and 76.7% on Core USDC, and exceeded 100% on Plasma USDT0 and Arbitrum WETH. This headroom is available to any borrower at any time, including one holding stolen or unbacked collateral, so a static cap limits the total that can be borrowed but places no limit on the pace at which it is borrowed.

In the largest malicious draws of the period, tens of millions of dollars of WETH were borrowed on Ethereum Core within minutes, alongside a parallel draw on Arbitrum, and each draw completed at full size before an emergency response took effect.

Characteristics of organic demand

A rate limit is only viable if it accommodates legitimate demand, which on Aave varies widely in both size and timing.

Reserve sizes span three orders of magnitude, from about $2M of debt on Mantle USDT0 early in the year to several billion on the Core stablecoins. A buffer that leaves comfortable room on a $10M reserve would be negligible on a $3B one, while a buffer sized for Core would leave a small reserve effectively unconstrained, so the buffer has to scale with the reserve.

Organic demand also arrives in bursts. Measured as the largest amount borrowed within any 60-minute window of each day, Core USDT exceeded $25M on 84 days of the year and $50M on 32, Core USDC on 67 and 28 days, and Core WETH on 69 and 24, so refills on the largest reserves have to keep pace with bursts of this size.

Individual borrows can be very large as well. Over the year, Core USDT recorded 78 transactions borrowing $25M or more, Core WETH 68 and Core USDC 49, with the largest at $190M. A significant share of these comes from integrated institutional clients and large loopers, whose flows resemble an attack in size (not in intent) and who typically want to enter the market and position themselves without delay. Continuing to serve these users with minimal friction remains a priority, which requires a pathway that accommodates them without reopening the room that the rate limit closes for everyone else.

Goals

The first stage of LlamaGuard Caps is designed to bound how quickly debt on any reserve can grow, so that a toxic flow is limited both in size and in speed, while leaving normal borrowing and the growth of the protocol largely unaffected. Borrowing room is refilled automatically as organic demand uses it, and integrated institutional clients and other known large borrowers retain a safe and predictable pathway to borrow at the size they need.

The same rule is meant to serve every Aave V3 instance, from reserves with a few million dollars of debt to Core reserves with several billion, and to operate on every reserve at all times, so that protection does not depend on recognising an attack while it is under way. These properties are delivered on the Risk Agents stack that Aave Governance already owns, with computation on Chainlink CRE and every bound enforced onchain. This also means that the functionality of the system can be extended flexibly, adding additional safeguards and modules on top of the initial implementation.

Design

LlamaGuard Caps relies on two agents that act on the same borrow cap. The Raise agent adds borrowing room as organic demand uses it, and the Cut agent removes room that repayments and liquidations reopen beyond what the reserve needs. Each agent can move the cap in one direction only as enforced onchain, and both work toward the same target, a cap that sits one buffer above the current debt of the reserve.

Rules

The buffer L is a share \alpha of the reserve’s debt D, bounded by a floor L_{\min} and a ceiling L_{\max}, so that it grows with the reserve while the amount that can be drawn in a single step remains limited on the largest markets. Both agents target the same cap,

C = D + L, \qquad L(D) = \max\big(L_{\min},\ \min(L_{\max},\ \alpha D)\big),

and the cap written onchain never exceeds the hard maximum \bar C (set by the Risk Stewards or governance as enforced by existing risk methodologies), nor the current supply cap S,

C^{\text{eff}} = \min\big(C,\ \bar C,\ S\big).

A borrow of x succeeds if D + x \le C^{\text{eff}}. Otherwise, the borrower waits for the next top-up, splits the borrow or uses one of the pathways described below.

The Raise agent tops up the cap once borrowing has used most of the buffer. If the free headroom B = C - D was at or below a trigger share \theta of the buffer one delay \tau earlier, the cap is reset to D + L, and no two top-ups on a reserve are closer than \tau. The delay converts the cap from a limit on size into a limit on pace, since a borrower who exhausts the buffer must wait before further room opens. The Cut agent acts in the opposite case. When a repayment or liquidation leaves headroom more than a band \delta above the buffer, it returns the cap to D + L within one or two blocks, so that repaid room does not accumulate as open capacity, while smaller repayments leave the cap unchanged and the repaid amount available to borrow again.

Agent Condition Action Timing
Raise agent headroom one delay earlier was B \le \theta L C \leftarrow D + L(D) at least \tau after the previous top-up
Cut agent B > (1+\delta)L after a repayment or liquidation C \leftarrow D + L(D) within one or two blocks

Starting from a full buffer, the debt of one reserve can therefore rise by L at once and by one further L per top-up. Within T of the first borrow, after a period in which headroom stayed above \theta L, the most one reserve can grow is

(1+\delta)L + L\lfloor T/\tau \rfloor

If headroom was already at or below \theta L one delay before a draw, a top-up is due as the draw starts and the reserve can receive two buffers in quick succession. The bound then becomes (2+\delta)L + L\lfloor T/\tau \rfloor, which is also the worst case the on-chain checks allow should the raise workflow misbehave.

Pathways for large borrowers and institutional clients

The main trade-off of a rate limit falls on large and persistent borrowers who want to enter the market and position themselves immediately, with sizes well above the buffer that suits the median user. Sizing the buffer to their needs would leave the same room open to an attacker, so the buffer stays at the scale of typical demand, and known large borrowers, including integrated institutional clients, still keep dedicated pathways through which the Risk Stewards can open exactly the room a borrow needs in the transaction that uses it, without defeating the purpose of a rate limit.

  1. Split across top-ups. By default, a borrow larger than the buffer is split across top-ups with no action required from governance, so a borrow of three buffers is admitted as one buffer immediately and the remainder over the next two top-ups.
  2. Atomic batch. Known large borrowers that cannot wait, including integrated institutional clients, can be served through a batch executed by the Risk Stewards, in which the cap is raised by the exact amount of the borrow and the new room is consumed in the same transaction.
  3. Hold. For new onboardings and periods of genuine sustained demand, in which the cap itself would otherwise bind, the Risk Stewards can raise the cap together with a hold of limited duration, during which the Cut agent leaves the raised cap in place. Holds are scheduled only in these cases, since a hold leaves the raised room open to any user for its duration.

Flash loans repaid within the same transaction do not count against the borrow cap, so refinancing and collateral swaps that close within one transaction are unaffected. Atomic leverage loops continue to work as long as the debt opened in one transaction fits under the headroom, and known large loopers can use the atomic batch.

Large suppliers remain unaffected at this stage. Supply caps keep their current configuration and deposits of any size continue to enter as they do today, limited by the general risk exposure caps where applicable.

Architecture & roles

Both agents reuse the AaveBorrowCapAgent code on the Risk Agents stack that Aave Governance already owns, and Aave’s core contracts, AgentHub, the RiskOracle and the Router remain unchanged. The system adds four contracts, a Chainlink CRE workflow and a keeper. The audit will cover the four new contracts and the raise workflow. Each raise is delivered as a signed report through Chainlink’s forwarder and the Router to the RiskOracle, and AgentHub executes it through the Raise agent. A cut is computed onchain from live Aave state.

Component Status Role Bounded by
Raise workflow new CRE workflow computes and signs raises module rule, AgentHub \tau
Keeper planned offchain service triggers due cuts module rule; anyone can trigger
CapsRangeValidationModuleV3 new contract checks every agent raise and cut Executor-set limits
CapsReducerOracle new contract adminless view returning the cut the module accepts module re-check at execution
CapsParameterRegistry new contract trigger, margin (a deduction from D + L or S that absorbs small repayments), asset lists and switches read offchain only; module rule
CapsBorrowForwarder new contract atomic cap raise and borrow for the Risk Council Safe Risk Steward limits, \bar C
Raise agent, Cut agent existing AaveBorrowCapAgent code, one deployment per Pool, the only new holder of the Pool’s RISK_ADMIN role write caps through AgentHub; one registration raises, the other cuts module rule, AgentHub \tau
Aave core, AgentHub, RiskOracle, Router existing, no code change one raise route for this workflow, with Router step and delay limits disabled as the module bounds each raise, and two registrations unchanged

A raise from the Raise agent requires at least \tau since that agent’s previous raise on the reserve, a reserve neither frozen nor paused, and a new cap above the current one and at most \min(D + L,\ \bar C,\ S) in the executing block. The module does not check the trigger. Whatever the workflow signs, each raise stays within one buffer above live debt, at most once per \tau. AgentHub enforces \tau, and the AIP registers one Raise and one Cut agent per Pool with the Protocol Guardian as agent admin. The module computes each cut onchain from live Aave state and accepts it only within the band. A cut can only lower a cap, and low caps block only new borrows.

Both checks run in CapsRangeValidationModuleV3, which plugs into the unchanged agent and applies one rule to raises and cuts, evaluated against live Aave state in the executing block. With the standard module, which checks only step size, the offchain workflow would be trusted for the size of every raise. Here the workflow proposes a value and the module decides whether it may be written. A rejected update is skipped without reverting, so it cannot block other markets. Cuts continue during a freeze or pause.

Role Holder Can do

Summary

LlamaRisk is building Aave’s Risk Layer: automated risk solutions that make expert risk judgment verifiable, with every parameter, bound and action checkable onchain. The Aave Risk Framework set this direction in June by making continuous risk oracles part of the protocol’s standing infrastructure. Governance and manual review can trail a fast-moving event by hours, and the evolution of AI capabilities keeps shortening the time between finding a weakness and exploiting it, so protection has to run continuously and at machine speed. LlamaGuard PT went live in September as the first of these solutions. We continue the rollout with LlamaGuard Caps as the next addition.

Aave’s greatest strength is its liquidity, deep enough to move capital instantly and at scale. Defending access to that liquidity programmatically protects Aave’s users, even when a failure elsewhere in DeFi puts compromised collateral or stolen assets in play. LlamaGuard Caps hardens Aave’s perimeter. Its first stage, a borrow rate limiter for Aave V3, gives each reserve a margin of borrowing room above its debt, sized to the reserve. That room refills automatically as organic demand uses it and is cut back when large repayments open up more than the reserve needs. Everyday borrowing keeps instant access to liquidity. A large draw, though, has to wait for each refill, giving the Protocol Guardian reasonable time to respond to illegitimate activity. Integrated institutional clients and other approved large borrowers will have a dedicated pathway that meets their capital demand quickly.

LlamaGuard Caps will run on the Risk Agents stack that Aave Governance already owns. Raises are computed on Chainlink CRE, on the same oracle network that delivers the price feeds Aave relies on, and every bound is enforced onchain. Aave’s core contracts and existing agents stay unchanged, and the new smart contract surface is small. Every lever stays with Aave governance: Risk Stewards and governance continue to set each cap’s maximum, and automation controls only how fast room opens beneath it. This proposal is the first stage of a gradual rollout. Later stages will set the ceiling itself from live liquidity conditions and extend dynamic protection to supply caps, Aave V4 and cross-market modules, each calibrated on live data from the stage before.

Threat model

Two external threats have proved the most consequential for Aave.

  1. An attacker deposits maliciously obtained collateral that is worth less than the oracle reports, and borrows against it.
  2. An attacker gains control of many different assets, deposits them as collateral and borrows assets that can’t be frozen, as fast as possible.

In both cases the damage starts outside Aave, with a compromised asset or a compromised holder. Aave is affected because its deep, instant liquidity is what the attacker needs to turn that position into assets that can leave. Aave can’t prevent these events. It can control how quickly its liquidity is drawn once one is under way, and so how much time the Protocol Guardian has to investigate and respond.

Exposure under static caps

Borrow caps on Aave are set by the Risk Stewards or through governance AIPs. Each change is generated programmatically but still needs human approval, through the Risk Steward multisig or a governance vote, and must wait out a minimum delay before the next one. A cap therefore has to hold enough room for the growth expected before its next revision. That headroom is open by design. Over the year from October 2025 to October 2026, standing borrow headroom averaged 41.1% of debt on Core WETH, 75.3% on Core USDT and 76.7% on Core USDC, and exceeded 100% on Plasma USDT0 and Arbitrum WETH. This headroom is available to any borrower at any time, including one holding stolen or unbacked collateral, so a static cap limits the total that can be borrowed but places no limit on the pace at which it is borrowed.

In the largest malicious draws of the period, tens of millions of dollars of WETH were borrowed on Ethereum Core within minutes, alongside a parallel draw on Arbitrum, and each draw completed at full size before an emergency response took effect.

Characteristics of organic demand

A rate limit is only viable if it accommodates legitimate demand, which on Aave varies widely in both size and timing.

Reserve sizes span three orders of magnitude, from about $2M of debt on Mantle USDT0 early in the year to several billion on the Core stablecoins. A buffer that leaves comfortable room on a $10M reserve would be negligible on a $3B one, while a buffer sized for Core would leave a small reserve effectively unconstrained, so the buffer has to scale with the reserve.

Organic demand also arrives in bursts. Measured as the largest amount borrowed within any 60-minute window of each day, Core USDT exceeded $25M on 84 days of the year and $50M on 32, Core USDC on 67 and 28 days, and Core WETH on 69 and 24, so refills on the largest reserves have to keep pace with bursts of this size.

Individual borrows can be very large as well. Over the year, Core USDT recorded 78 transactions borrowing $25M or more, Core WETH 68 and Core USDC 49, with the largest at $190M. A significant share of these comes from integrated institutional clients and large loopers, whose flows resemble an attack in size (not in intent) and who typically want to enter the market and position themselves without delay. Continuing to serve these users with minimal friction remains a priority, which requires a pathway that accommodates them without reopening the room that the rate limit closes for everyone else.

Goals

The first stage of LlamaGuard Caps is designed to bound how quickly debt on any reserve can grow, so that a toxic flow is limited both in size and in speed, while leaving normal borrowing and the growth of the protocol largely unaffected. Borrowing room is refilled automatically as organic demand uses it, and integrated institutional clients and other known large borrowers retain a safe and predictable pathway to borrow at the size they need.

The same rule is meant to serve every Aave V3 instance, from reserves with a few million dollars of debt to Core reserves with several billion, and to operate on every reserve at all times, so that protection does not depend on recognising an attack while it is under way. These properties are delivered on the Risk Agents stack that Aave Governance already owns, with computation on Chainlink CRE and every bound enforced onchain. This also means that the functionality of the system can be extended flexibly, adding additional safeguards and modules on top of the initial implementation.

Design

LlamaGuard Caps relies on two agents that act on the same borrow cap. The Raise agent adds borrowing room as organic demand uses it, and the Cut agent removes room that repayments and liquidations reopen beyond what the reserve needs. Each agent can move the cap in one direction only as enforced onchain, and both work toward the same target, a cap that sits one buffer above the current debt of the reserve.

The buffer L is a share \alpha of the reserve’s debt D, bounded by a floor L_{\min} and a ceiling L_{\max}, so that it grows with the reserve while the amount that can be drawn in a single step remains limited on the largest markets. Both agents target the same cap,

C = D + L, \qquad L(D) = \max\big(L_{\min},\ \min(L_{\max},\ \alpha D)\big),

C^{\text{eff}} = \min\big(C,\ \bar C,\ S\big).

A borrow of x succeeds if D + x \le C^{\text{eff}}. Otherwise, the borrower waits for the next top-up, splits the borrow or uses one of the pathways described below.

governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

Aave V3 Core:

  • Increase borrow cap for USDC from 2,750,000,000 to 2,950,000,000.

USDC (Aave V3 Core)

USDC has reached 99.0% borrow cap utilization (2.72B / 2.75B) on the Aave V3 Core instance.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 12, 2026

The top 20 USDC borrowers run health factors between 1.02 and 3.03 with a median of 1.75, and the largest borrower accounts for about 14% of outstanding debt. Collateral behind these positions is mainly ETH and BTC assets, with 6 of the 20 posting weETH, 5 cbBTC, 5 WETH, 4 wstETH, and 3 WBTC, alongside 2 posting USDe and 2 sUSDe, so HF in the cohort tracks the ETH and BTC prices and, on the USDe and sUSDe positions, the exchange rate of those assets against the stablecoin debt.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the borrow cap from 2.75B to 2.95B on Aave V3 Core, which places the reserve at approximately 92.3% post-change borrow cap utilization. Reserve utilization stands at 95.6%, above the 94% optimal point, and the proposed borrow cap exceeds current supply of 2.85B, so additional borrowing remains bounded by available liquidity of approximately 126M USDC.

governance_posts.title: Introducing AaveAPY: An Yield Dashboard and Simulator
governance_posts.description:
Hi fellow Aave community members,

I am sharing with you an open-source analytics dashboard and simulator that I have been building: AaveAPY.

Live Dashboard: aaveapy.com
Code Source: github.com/0xPabloLI/aaveapy

Key Features

AaveAPY operates as an analytics layer on top of Aave V3.

1. Omni-Chain Yield Comparison

Instead of switching networks, AaveAPY displays a consolidated table showing Native APY + Incentive APY (including points calculator). You can instantly spot the best yield opportunities, filter by asset type, and identify markets with the strongest Supply APY − Borrow APY spread for looping strategies.

2. “What-If” Simulation with On-Chain Protocol Math

Enter a hypothetical supply or borrow amount to simulate the exact impact on your rates. The calculator uses Aave’s native on-chain math (two-slope curve) to show:

  • Supply/borrow APR/APY at the new utilization rate
  • Distance from the optimal utilization (kink) point
  • Remaining borrow cap room and pool liquidity constraints

3. Real Yield After Incentive Caps & Dilution

AaveAPY simulates your actual APY after accounting for incentive caps and dilution, for example:

  • Celo Self-Authentication: Factors in the $1,000 cap per user
  • Merkl/Brevis Forecasts: Estimates the next-run daily rewards and APR for hypothetical deposit amounts based on different campaign type and finite reward pools
  • INK FDV Calculator: Estimate Ink incentive APR based on different Fully Diluted Valuation assumptions

Roadmap

  • Aave V4 protocol support with unified V3/V4 frontend display
  • Complex simulation scenarios across different supply/borrow combinations
  • Smart deployment recommendation with multi-chain yield optimization and cross-chain bridge integration
  • Wallet connection with portfolio import and incentive blacklist/whitelist detection

I built this tool for my own needs, but I hope it brings value to the broader Aave community. Any of your feedback is appreciated.

Enjoy!

governance_posts.title: Introducing zyk-positions — understand what your Aave V3 position is actually doing
governance_posts.description:
Hello Aave Community

I’ve been using Aave V3 for a while and kept running into the same problem: the UI shows you numbers but never explains what they actually mean or what you should do next. Health factor 1.05 — is that dangerous or fine? Depends entirely on what you’re holding and why, and nothing tells you that.

So I built zyk-positions.

How it works

-– Paste any wallet address (read-only, no connection needed)
— Full position breakdown: collateral, debt, health factor, liquidation price, P&L over time, full transaction history
— AI analysis that explains the strategy in plain English and identifies the actual risk drivers
— What-if simulator: drag collateral prices or input repay/add amounts and watch HF, net worth and debt update live


Position overview and live what-if simulator — drag collateral price to see HF update in real time


Full transaction history with USD values at time of transaction

What it actually does differently

Example I found recently: a wallet running a weETH/WETH correlated loop at 10.4x leverage, HF 1.05. Looks like a liquidation waiting to happen. The AI identified it’s in E-Mode — the real liquidation trigger isn’t an ETH price move at all, it’s a weETH depeg of just 4.9%. Completely different risk than the number alone suggests.


AI analysis identifying E-Mode and the real liquidation trigger

Full example: 0x1DF1…37E8 · Aave V3 · Zyk Positions

Current state

-– Aave V3 mainnet only, alpha
— Free, no account needed

Would love feedback from people actively managing positions — especially edge cases where the analysis misses something or gets it wrong.

Deep analysis of Aave V3 positions — current state, full history, AI narrative.

governance_posts.title: Unauthorized sweep of staked Aave positions: drainer address 0x413e4f4d…706da, 8 Nov 2026
governance_posts.description:
Greetings

On 2026-11-08 at 18:10:35 UTC two Aave-related token positions held by our wallet 0x64cacba2bca8785961c450b928dc60b03742b3cc were transferred out without our authorization. We did not sign these transactions, and we were not at the device at the time.

The destination 0x413e4f4de7e5ff010913488f781e679e76f706da looks like a large automated sweeper, not an exchange and not a wallet of ours.

We are posting to (1) warn other users, (2) ask whether anyone recognises this pattern, and (3) request any guidance the Aave community or service providers can offer on evidence collection for a criminal complaint.

Affected positions

Token Contract Amount Value at time of theft
AUSDT (Aave Ethereum USDT, aToken) 0x23878914efe38d27c4d67ab83ed1b93a74d4086a 10,028.528651 ≈ $10,015.77
stkwaEthUSDC.v1 (Umbrella Stake Wrapped Aave Ethereum USDC v1) 0x6bf183243fdd1e306ad2c4450bc7dcf6f0bf8aa6 8,398.570816 ≈ $9,238.43

Total: ≈ $19,254 USD.

Both positions had been held in this wallet since 2026-06-26 and were stable until the transfer.

Transactions (Ethereum mainnet)

# Tx hash Token Amount Destination Time (UTC)
1 0x5223f78b9300ec6fa2c6cb2ead79b3527857be2ccc1374f5d88c647c24d8fd44 stkwaEthUSDC.v1 8,398.570816 0x413e4f4de7e5ff010913488f781e679e76f706da 2026-11-08 18:10:35
2 0x254c93130dd20f21db96c39ba29a8847f9b7eb148e4664c40bf429d2421693b4 AUSDT 10,028.528651 0x413e4f4de7e5ff010913488f781e679e76f706da 2026-11-08 18:10:35
3 0xdcc81d176c246f3c6365fee6b7a49f6321eada7df4c4cae2a5b40cd212a5497a unverified ERC-20 (placeholder in our indexer) 10,028.528651 0x413e1868ecefa385b5c1c16421dd19a01e1806da 2026-11-08 18:17:47
4 0x4157f599d1589defd84ae0503dc60772ee91239ced66836074be637ec3de735d AUSDT 0 (residual) 0x413e1868ecefa385b5c1c16421dd19a01e1806da 2026-11-08 18:17:59

Transactions 1 and 2 were both plain transfer() calls (selector 0xa9059cbb) from the victim wallet (ours) to the drainer, mined in the same block.

Transactions 3 and 4 are NOT attributable to the same actor in the same way and we flag them separately: in tx 3 the from field on-chain is 0x1584a8ee67789d1fe161065388657ad2f2a3c7dd and in tx 4 it is 0xd6434d157f254276d69ede3bd9fc805482206908. Neither is our wallet. Our indexer had initially mis-attributed them to us; a direct chain read corrected this. We list them because the amount in tx 3 exactly equals the stolen AUSDT balance, which we cannot yet explain.

Balance state

  • Victim wallet 0x64cacba2…b3cc, AUSDT: 10,027.88 → 0.001219 (residual base-unit dust).
  • Victim wallet, stkwaEthUSDC.v1: 8,398.570816 → 0.
  • Neither position has returned. There is no inbound transaction restoring either token.

The destination address: why we call it a sweeper

0x413e4f4de7e5ff010913488f781e679e76f706da

We retrieved its full transfer history from a public indexer. It is not an exchange deposit address, not a bridge, and not contract code (eth_getCode returns empty, it is an EOA). Its behaviour:

  • 1,810 inbound transactions, 644 token transfers, zero outbound token transfers as of 2026-11-11. It only receives.
  • Nonce = 0. It has never signed a transaction of its own. It is funded and operated indirectly.
  • 326 distinct sending addresses across 91 distinct tokens (USDC, WETH, USDT, INJ, stETH, eETH, AAVE, ENA, PENDLE, ONDO, LINK, DAI, UNI, and 78 more).
  • Active since 2026-11-07 17:50 UTC, i.e. it was already sweeping other wallets before it took our positions on 2026-11-08.
  • Transfers arrive in synchronised waves at 12-second intervals (18:09:47 → 18:10:11 → 18:10:35 → 18:10:59 → 18:11:11 → 18:11:47 …), consistent with an automated bot rather than manual operation.
  • It currently holds 13.9558 ETH of native balance, presumably consolidated from victims.

Within the same 2-minute window as our loss, this address also received ONDO from 0x1C84ed8A20949B48e1404e8c9F23FCBeD5B1C20d, HOLD and NPC from 0x32D396E179f9fF3Fa002091AE0C27F23fEa04B80, LINK from 0xf946a0371F031900575d36ede1B934BE8C5899E1, TRAC from 0x6cE51890484D5e37b85E3b865F238EF115DE5FC5, and ONDO from 0xa5A50E4aFd4Bdd071472486086B322c67E31889f.

If you recognise any of those addresses as yours, you are likely a victim of the same operator. Please check.

Suspected access vector

We believe the signing key was compromised through illicit access to the machine on which the wallet browser extension was installed. Our working hypothesis involves a Keplr installation:

  • Our hypothesis is therefore either (a) the same mnemonic was imported into a Cosmos wallet and into an Ethereum wallet on the same machine, so a single seed compromise reached both, or (b) the compromise is in an Ethereum extension (or in the seed material stored on disk) and Keplr is a correlated symptom, not the vector.
  • We are still determining which. We are not claiming a Keplr vulnerability, and we are not claiming Aave was involved in any way. Aave contracts behaved correctly: it was a plain token transfer authorised by a key we no longer control.

We are aware this is the standard profile of commodity infostealer malware (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar and similar families) that harvests browser extension storage and seed phrases. We have not yet completed a forensic image of the device.

What we are asking

  1. Has anyone seen 0x413e4f4de7e5ff010913488f781e679e76f706da in other reports? Any prior thread, any Aave forum post, any public tag: we want to link this to a broader campaign.
  2. Is there any asset-side action available for stkwaEthUSDC.v1 or AUSDT? We understand a signed transfer() is irreversible and that neither you nor the Aave contracts can reverse it. We are asking whether there is any pause, freeze, or blacklist mechanism on these specific token contracts that a legitimate issuer could invoke and whether such a mechanism has ever been used in practice.
  3. Does the Aave service provider set (Chaos Labs, LlamaRisk, BGD Labs, TokenLogic) publish or accept drainer-address intelligence that we could contribute to? We would rather hand the address to a body that tracks it than see it posted only in a support thread.
  4. Has anyone had a transfer() from a stkwa*/Umbrella token recovered or clawed back by any means whatsoever? We would like to know whether it is truly 0%.

We want to be candid: we are not posting this expecting recovery. We are posting because the address is still active, it took six more wallets in our window alone, it has taken from 326 addresses in total, and it will take more. If this thread makes one person check their device today, it was worth writing.

What we are doing on our side

  • Taking the affected machine offline pending forensic examination.
  • Migrating all remaining holdings that shared the compromised seed material to newly generated keys on hardware that has never touched the compromised environment.
  • Preserving a full database and chain export of the incident before making any corrections to our own indexer, so the evidence set stays intact.

We will update this thread with the results of the device forensics when available.

Thank you for reading, and please check your own extension wallets.

What we are doing on our side

  • Taking the affected machine offline pending forensic examination.
  • Migrating all remaining holdings that shared the compromised seed material to newly generated keys on hardware that has never touched the compromised environment.
  • Preserving a full database and chain export of the incident before making any corrections to our own indexer, so the evidence set stays intact.

We will update this thread with the results of the device forensics when available.

Thank you for reading, and please check your own extension wallets.

governance_posts.title: [ARFC] Extend HyperLend's Friendly Fork Recognition to Elysium (Aave v3.7)
governance_posts.description:
Author: HyperLend Team
Date: 2026-11-06

Summary

This proposal seeks Aave DAO recognition of a new HyperLend deployment as a friendly fork of Aave, on Elysium, Kinetiq’s Layer 2 for the Hyperliquid ecosystem.

The deployment will use the Aave v3.7 codebase and will consist only of Aave pools. HyperLend will share 50% of all revenue generated by the Elysium deployment with the Aave DAO. The remaining 50% will be used to buy back HyperLend’s token, HPL.

Block Analitica will continue to serve as risk manager.

Motivation

HyperLend’s track record

In early 2025, the Aave DAO recognized HyperLend as a friendly fork on HyperEVM (TEMP CHECK, ARFC). Since then, HyperLend has:

  • Originated approximately $2B in loans (Block Analitica dashboard)

  • Reached a peak total market size of over $900M (Block Analitica dashboard), and currently holds over $530M in TVL with $250M in active loans (DefiLlama)

  • Operated securely and at scale for more than a year

  • Worked continuously with Block Analitica on risk management

We believe this record shows HyperLend can run an Aave-based money market responsibly. We want to bring that experience to a second network.

Why Elysium

Elysium is a high-throughput Arbitrum Orbit L2 built by Kinetiq. It settles to HyperEVM, runs co-located with HyperCore, and uses HYPE as gas. It is designed for higher-frequency onchain activity than HyperEVM can support.

As liquidity and trading activity grow on Elysium, demand for a reliable money market will follow. HyperLend intends to capture that flow, and this proposal ensures the Aave DAO shares directly in it.

Benefits to the Aave DAO

  • 50% of all revenue from the Elysium deployment, with no exclusions, compared with 10% under our original HyperEVM terms

  • Expansion of the Aave codebase into the Hyperliquid L2 ecosystem with no DAO capital or operational burden

  • An operator with an established track record, an existing relationship with the DAO, and a continuing risk partner

Specification

We propose that HyperLend:

  • Deploy Aave v3.7 on Elysium as a friendly fork operated by HyperLend

  • Offer only Aave pools on Elysium (no isolated pools, P2P, or other products)

  • Share 50% of all revenue generated by the Elysium deployment with the Aave DAO, distributed either monthly or through a RevenueSplitter contract

  • Use the remaining 50% of Elysium revenue to buy back HPL

  • Retain Block Analitica as risk manager for the Elysium deployment

  • Deploy as soon as this proposal passes governance

No token allocation is included in this proposal. The revenue share is the DAO’s compensation.

In return, the Aave DAO should:

  • Grant HyperLend a license to use the Aave v3.7 codebase on Elysium

  • Notify HyperLend of potential security issues in the Aave codebase so they can be mitigated before public disclosure

Next Steps

  1. Gather feedback from the Aave community

  2. Escalate to an ARFC Snapshot

  3. If the ARFC passes, deploy on Elysium

governance_posts.title: [Direct-to-AIP] Reserve Factor Updates Across Aave V3 and V2 Markets
governance_posts.description:
title: [Direct-to-AIP] Reserve Factor Updates Across Aave V3 and V2 Markets
author: @TokenLogic
created: 2026-11-12

Summary

This publication proposes Reserve Factor updates on 54 reserves across 12 Aave V3 instances and the Aave V2 Ethereum market. At balances and rates as of 9 November 2026, the changes add about $3.5M of annualised revenue to the DAO and raise the blended RF from 12.0% to 12.7%. The proposal is part of the ongoing effort to streamline Aave V3.

Motivation

Overview

Over the past months, the DAO has been streamlining Aave V3. Low-adoption reserves and instances have been wound down, Aave V2 has been frozen, and ongoing work aims to focus Ethereum Core on liquid, bluechip collateral, with assets that carry additional risk moving to Aave V4, where that risk can be priced. This proposal applies the same direction to the protocol’s revenue side.

Every borrowable reserve exposes the DAO to collateral, oracle and liquidation risk. The RF compensates the DAO for carrying that risk. On many reserves today, the DAO keeps a small share of the interest on positions whose tail risk it fully underwrites. Raising the RF improves the DAO’s return for the same risk, without changing the rate any borrower pays. On legacy markets, it also lowers the incentive to keep liquidity where activity is being wound down.

TokenLogic has reviewed the RF of every borrowable reserve across Aave V3 and V2. Reserves not listed in the Specification keep their current RF. The RF decides how the interest paid by borrowers is split between suppliers and the DAO; it does not change the rate a borrower pays. Its effect therefore depends on who the reserve’s users are:

  • On stablecoins, suppliers choose a venue on supply APY, so the RF is a competitive parameter first. On V3, stablecoin RFs in this proposal stay at or below 70%, except for DAI.e on Avalanche, and most move by 5 to 15 percentage points.
  • On assets with very low utilisation (BTC wrappers, LSTs and LRTs), the supply APY is already ~0.00%, and most debt is in old positions, with several on reserves where borrowing is already disabled. Raising the RF there costs suppliers at most 1-2 bps.
  • On markets in decline, or where users have a better Aave alternative on the same chain, a higher RF directs activity to the markets the DAO wants to grow.

The changes below are grouped by rationale. Revenue figures are annualised at borrow balances and rates as of 9 November 2026. Ethereum Core WETH is not included, so that its parameters can be coordinated with the ongoing work on Ethereum Core collateral.

Rationale: Assets with no Supply Yield (to 100%)

Network Asset Current RF New RF Borrowed Supply APY change (bps) Revenue change (/yr)
Ethereum Core WBTC 50% 100% $51,959,854 0 $81,503
Ethereum Core cbBTC 50% 100% $9,318,184 0 $13,293
Ethereum Core wstETH 35% 100% $30,915,857 0 $3,766
Ethereum Core weETH 45% 100% $114,545 0 $634
Ethereum Core tBTC 50% 100% $186,835 0 $241
Ethereum Core FBTC 75% 100% $75,236 0 $105
Ethereum Core cbETH 15% 100% $38,534 0 $22
Ethereum Core rETH 15% 100% $101,549 0 $16

Base cbETH 15% 100% $75,043 0 $5
Base wstETH 5% 100% $250,876 0 $16
Base weETH 45% 100% $6,220 0 $35
Arbitrum WBTC 50% 100% $10,011,686 -2 $35,812
Arbitrum weETH 45% 100% $4,384 0 $24

Avalanche WBTC.e 50% 100% $135,636 -2 $606

BNB Chain BTCB 20% 100% $904,465 -1 $4,897
Optimism WBTC 50% 100% $790,494 -2 $3,159
Optimism wstETH 5% 100% $83,828 0 $229
X Layer xBTC 10% 100% $2,765 0 $0

These reserves combine utilisation of a few percent with a supply APY that rounds to zero. Borrowing here is incidental (for example, a temporary hedge when the WETH borrow rate spikes), and no supplier is pricing in the yield. Setting the RF to 100% routes the full interest to the DAO with no effect on borrowers. Combined impact: +$173,209/yr.

Rationale: Volatile Tokens (to 50%)

Network Asset Current RF New RF Borrowed Supply APY change (bps) Revenue change (/yr)
Ethereum Core LINK 20% 50% $4,430,215 -1 $11,291
Arbitrum ARB 20% 50% $291,148 -3 $1,107
Arbitrum LINK 20% 50% $71,259 0 $71
Polygon WPOL 20% 50% $1,516,280 -25 $10,786
Gnosis GNO 20% 50% $351,657 -1 $1,000

LINK, ARB, WPOL, and GNO suppliers do not supply for yield, which is under 10 bps on LINK, ARB, and GNO and about 0.7% on WPOL. We propose 50% on all four. Combined impact: +$24,255/yr.

Rationale: USDe on Plasma

Network Asset Current RF New RF Borrowed Supply APY change (bps) Revenue change (/yr)
Plasma USDe 25% 35% $29,975,577 -4 $217,872

USDe borrow demand on Plasma is low (about 6% utilisation), and the USDe borrow rate currently sits above the sUSDe staking yield. The supply APY moves by 4 bps. Impact: +$217,872/yr.

Rationale: Plasma USDT0 and GHO

Network Asset Current RF New RF Borrowed Supply APY change (bps) Revenue change (/yr)
Plasma USDT0 5% 7.5% $632,468,070 -16 $1,036,635
Plasma GHO 5% 10% $18,382,445 -20 $42,678
  • USDT0: the RF moves from 5% to 7.5%, in line with the terms agreed with the Plasma team. This line will only be included in the AIP once those terms are finalised.
  • GHO: GHO on Plasma is supplied by users, and the DAO co-funds the incentives on this market. A 10% RF aligns it with GHO on Monad and Base.

Combined impact: +$1,079,313/yr.

Rationale: Ethereum Core DAI

Network Asset Current RF New RF Borrowed Supply APY change (bps) Revenue change (/yr)
Ethereum Core DAI 25% 30% $99,817,583 -17 $217,486

Ethereum Core DAI has about $127M supplied and $100M borrowed, at 78.5% utilisation. DAI supply on Ethereum Core has remained stable through recent changes in the USDS savings rate and in competing DAI rates. We propose a 5 percentage point increase, which lowers the supply APY by about 17 bps, from 2.6% to 2.4%. Impact: +$217,486/yr.

Rationale: Avalanche

Network Asset Current RF New RF Borrowed Supply APY change (bps) Revenue change (/yr)
Avalanche WAVAX 20% 50% $52,919,721 -38 $532,443
Avalanche USDC 10% 25% $60,960,281 -61 $416,862
Avalanche USDt 10% 25% $22,645,837 -78 $193,282
Avalanche DAI.e 25% 90% $2,115,720 -173 $53,383
Avalanche WETH.e 15% 50% $2,771,444 -2 $3,447

Aave V4 is live on Avalanche, where the same assets earn supply incentives. We propose a larger increase on the V3 market so that its economics reflect the V4 alternative. USDC and USDt move to 25%, WAVAX moves to 50% in line with the volatile tokens above, and DAI.e, a bridged legacy reserve, moves to 90%. Combined impact: +$1,199,417/yr.

Rationale: Polygon

Network Asset Current RF New RF Borrowed Supply APY change (bps) Revenue change (/yr)
Polygon USDT0 25% 30% $21,781,874 -25 $78,910
Polygon USDC 20% 25% $17,447,981 -24 $61,193
Polygon DAI 25% 70% $2,656,890 -270 $94,373
Polygon WETH 15% 25% $9,093,664 -6 $17,308

Polygon activity on Aave has been declining. We propose a moderate increase on USDT0, USDC and WETH, and a larger one on DAI, which is a legacy reserve on this network. Combined impact: +$251,784/yr.

Rationale: Optimism, Gnosis, Linea and BNB Chain

Network Asset Current RF New RF Borrowed Supply APY change (bps) Revenue change (/yr)
BNB Chain ETH 15% 25% $7,729,270 -7 $11,544
Optimism USDC 10% 15% $9,524,587 -42 $42,472
Optimism WETH 15% 20% $13,247,105 -7 $11,871
Optimism USDT 10% 15% $3,368,219 -21 $7,846
Gnosis EURe 10% 15% $11,546,910 -19 $26,988
Gnosis USDC.e 10% 20% $1,647,357 -38 $7,233
Linea WETH 15% 20% $3,966,775 -7 $4,044
Linea USDC 10% 15% $1,066,376 -34 $3,899

These are small markets with limited growth. We propose 5 to 10 percentage point increases on their main reserves; supply APY decreases by 7 to 42 bps. Stablecoin reserves on BNB Chain are unchanged. Combined impact: +$115,896/yr.

Rationale: Ethereum Prime wstETH

Network Asset Current RF New RF Borrowed Supply APY change (bps) Revenue change (/yr)
Ethereum Prime wstETH 5% 50% $37,549,348 -3 $32,337

wstETH utilisation on Prime is 31%, and its supply APY is 6 bps. Prime suppliers use wstETH as collateral and are not meaningfully exposed to the supply rate. Impact: +$32,337/yr.

Rationale: Aave V2 Ethereum

Network Asset Current RF New RF Borrowed Supply APY change (bps) Revenue change (/yr)
Ethereum V2 USDC 85% 99.99% $5,111,761 -40 $81,997
Ethereum V2 DAI 85% 99.99% $1,693,350 -33 $27,044
Ethereum V2 WETH 85% 99.99% $1,720,813 -16 $20,682
Ethereum V2 USDT 85% 99.99% $1,341,154 -22 $20,310
Ethereum V2 WBTC 90% 99.99% $114,307 -1 $2,542

Following the Aave V2 deprecation plan, all V2 Ethereum reserves are frozen, so suppliers cannot add liquidity and no new positions can open. We propose raising the RF on the remaining borrowed reserves from 85% (90% on WBTC) to 99.99%, directing nearly all remaining interest to the DAO. With no meaningful supply yield left, remaining suppliers have a reason to withdraw, which raises utilisation and the borrow rate and pushes open positions to close. Impact: +$152,574/yr.

Specification

governance_posts.description:

Considering the extreme centralization at custodian level, does the DAO think a custodian level limit makes sense? If not, why is the per-reserve sizing sufficient?

governance_posts.title: Aave Labs 180 Day Report
governance_posts.description:
Summary

Aave governance approved the Aave Will Win Framework in April 2026, and as part of that framework Aave Labs committed to publishing quarterly updates on its work as a service provider to the Aave DAO. This report combines the first the 180 days since that approval, spanning Q2 and Q3 2026.

Over the last 180 days, Aave Labs’ team of about 97 team members put an estimated 100,000 hours into its work for the Aave DAO and completed 6,096 tracked issues and 36 projects of various scopes across engineering, security, product, design, growth, marketing, governance, and legal. Over the same period, Aave Labs authored 26 onchain governance proposals and 20 Snapshot votes, and shipped 28 items including products, features, and protocol deployments. Aave Labs also prepared and implemented the DAO-approved onboarding of 33 unique assets, deployments on four new chains, and four new Aave V4 Liquidity Hubs with their corresponding Spokes.

Throughout Q2, Aave Labs assumed roughly 40 technical and supporting functions that BGD Labs and the Aave Chan Initiative (ACI) previously performed for the DAO, including contract maintenance, security coordination, proposal payload engineering, and developer tooling, and it completed both transitions while rsETH incident response (detailed below) was still underway.

Q3 was a strong quarter for launches and product expansion across the Aave ecosystem. Following DAO approval, Aave Labs implemented Aave V4 deployments on Avalanche, Arc, and Base, and V4 grew from $212.6 million deposits to $1.34 billion in Q3, passing its first $1 billion on September 16. Since launching from zero at the end of March, V4 has grown to more than $1.3 billion deposits in roughly six months. Aave App opened early access on iOS, expanded to five total chains, and launched instant onramps for eligible U.S. users through licensed third-party providers. We also opened up Stable Vaults, the vault infrastructure behind the Aave App, for enterprise use. Other key launches include the official Aave MCP server, which gives AI a direct connection to read Aave data and prepare transactions, the Aave V3 interface redesign, and the addition of each new V4 deployment to Aave Pro.

On the security side, Certora completed formal verification of core Aave V4 and Stable Vaults contracts against defined specifications, and three new V4 security audits were published over the period. Aave Labs coordinated these engagements, including scoping, remediation of findings, and fix review, before the final reports were published.

Aave Labs’ UK subsidiaries Push Labs Limited and Push Virtual Assets Limited (together, Push) were also registered with the Financial Conduct Authority as cryptoasset exchange providers. Push provides fiat on- and off-ramp services for eligible Aave App users.

Aave protocol revenue totaled $44.58 million across the 180 days, while deposits across all versions of the protocol grew by $9.69 billion in Q3 alone.

Incentive campaigns launched and supported 12 102 114

rsETH Response

On April 18 at 17:35 UTC, an exploit of the rsETH cross-chain bridge resulted in the release of 116,500 rsETH on Ethereum without a matching amount being burned on the source chain. The exploit did not involve the Aave Protocol’s smart contracts, which continued to operate as designed. The attacker supplied 89,567 of the stolen rsETH across eight Aave V3 positions and borrowed 82,650 WETH and 821 wstETH against it, after which the Aave Protocol Guardian froze the affected reserves within 85 minutes and the Risk Stewards made roughly 295 parameter changes across V3 reserves over the following weeks to contain exposure.

Aave Labs, TokenLogic, and LlamaRisk then helped coordinate DeFi United, a cross-protocol effort to restore rsETH’s backing for affected users. Within a week, Consensys and Joseph Lubin committed up to 30,000 ETH with strategic advice from SharpLink, Aave service providers proposed that Aave DAO contribute 25,000 ETH, and Golem contributed 1,000 ETH, while EtherFi, Ethena, Mantle, Frax, the Ink Foundation, Tydro, and LayerZero also joined the effort.

On April 25, Aave service providers, together with EtherFi, Kelp, LayerZero, Compound, and others, submitted a proposal asking the Arbitrum DAO to release into the recovery the ETH that the Arbitrum Security Council had frozen after the exploit. The vote reached quorum with more than 1,600 addresses representing over 190 million ARB. On May 1, a restraining notice was issued against the Arbitrum DAO in connection with an unrelated case. Following an application by Aave LLC, the court modified the notice on May 8 to allow the onchain vote and the transfer of the ETH to Aave LLC.

Aave governance executed AIP 478 on May 6, which liquidated the eight attacker positions without affecting any other users or Umbrella, Aave’s staking-based backstop. AIP 482 followed on May 16 and restored WETH borrowing limits to their pre-incident levels across the V3 Ethereum Core, Ethereum Prime, Arbitrum, Base, Mantle, and Linea markets. Kelp refilled the bridge with recovered rsETH across five tranches totaling 116,131.72 rsETH, which fully restored rsETH’s backing by May 26 and returned all Aave markets to normal operation.

Aave Labs prioritized its incident response work over its launch schedule and moved the affected launches into Q3. The public post mortem gives a fuller account of the response.

DAO Launches Overview

Aave Labs authored 26 onchain proposals and 20 Snapshot votes over the 180 days, and it submitted another 16 onchain proposals on behalf of other service providers. Onchain proposals are binding votes that execute code on the protocol, and Snapshot votes are offchain votes the DAO uses to approve a direction before the onchain step.

Aave Labs submitted the other 16 proposals in collaboration with TokenLogic, LlamaRisk, Chaos Labs, and Certora as part of the payload engineering function it took over from BGD Labs. A payload is the smart contract code that a proposal executes, and Aave Labs now writes, tests, and submits that code for other service providers in addition to its own proposals.

Aave Labs also published the Technical Asset Listing Framework to the governance forum on May 28, which sets one technical standard for every new asset listing, continued listing, and material parameter expansion across Aave V3, Aave V4, and Aave Horizon, along with requirements for ongoing monitoring of listed assets. The framework passed Snapshot in July and is now a formal part of the asset onboarding process.

Assets Onboarded

Aave Labs prepared the technical onboarding of 33 unique assets approved by the DAO over the 180 days, with six in Q2 and 27 in Q3. Eight came through standalone listing proposals, and 25 launched with the four new chain deployments. An asset that appears in more than one market, such as USDC, is counted once, in the first market where it was onboarded during the period.

Functions Absorbed from BGD Labs and ACI

During Q2, Aave Labs assumed roughly 40 technical and supporting functions from BGD Labs and ACI (with others taken on by TokenLogic), spanning developer tooling, security coordination, and governance infrastructure. Aave Labs now maintains the Aave Address Book, which is the official registry of every Aave contract address and deployment, the Aave Helpers, which are shared code libraries used across proposals, the Aave CLI, which is the command-line toolkit developers use to build on Aave, and the Aave Permission Book, which publicly documents the addresses that hold permissions on the protocol.

Aave Labs is also adapting the Correlated Assets Price Oracle (CAPO) to V4. CAPO limits how quickly the price of a yield-bearing asset such as wstETH can rise, which protects Aave markets from price manipulation.

Through the same transition, Aave Labs took on security coordination and vulnerability response support for V3 and earlier versions, along with ongoing contract maintenance for those versions and the deprecation of the legacy Safety Module. Aave Labs now prepares the technical deployment work for DAO-approved asset listings and chain launches across protocol versions, which over this period included the V3 Monad market and the V4 Avalanche, Arc, and Base deployments.

Babylon Integration

Native BTC loans, powered by Babylon’s Trustless Vaults, ran on V4 testnet in June, and the integration is now in audit with Certora, two independent researchers, and an internal Aave Labs review. Bringing native Bitcoin to V4 would unlock much more BTC collateral for Aave than currently exists inside the wrapped versions of the asset.

V4-Specific Security and Risk Management

Aave Labs’ smart contract security team led the security work on V4 over the 180 days. Alongside external audits, the team introduced AI-assisted code review across Aave Labs repositories and coordinated each external engagement through scoping, remediation, and fix review.

Aave Labs worked with Certora to formally verify the core V4 contracts in July, covering the Liquidity Hub, the Spoke, and the Tokenization Spoke contracts along with the math libraries they rely on. Formal verification uses mathematical proofs to check that code behaves according to a defined set of specifications. Aave Labs also worked with Sherlock on a new V4 security audit published May 26, and with ChainSecurity on two more, one on the Tokenization Spoke published June 19 and one on the Liquidity Hub, Spoke, and position manager contracts published July 21.

AIP 523, authored by Aave Labs and approved by the DAO, activated Risk Stewards on V4 on September 25. Risk Stewards allow risk service providers to raise or lower supply caps, borrow caps, and other risk settings within preset limits and waiting periods, so V4 can adjust to demand within days, with no separate DAO vote needed for each change.

Aave Labs also worked to integrate Chainlink SVR into Aave V4 markets for eligible assets. SVR, short for Smart Value Recapture, captures the profit that bots earn from liquidations and returns it to the DAO, and on V3 it has returned over $11 million to the DAO treasury since March 2025.

Aave App

Aave App opened to its first users through Ghost Passes on August 26, and since then users from around the world have started using the app, funding it with stablecoins or from their bank accounts through Push and licensed providers. Balances across all Aave App users have since crossed $45 million.

During Q3, Aave Labs added instant deposit onboarding for eligible U.S. users, provided through licensed providers, and expanded Aave App from one chain to five, adding Ethereum, Base, HyperEVM, and BNB Chain to Arbitrum so users can deposit stablecoins from any of those networks. Aave Labs also spent Q3 developing the Android version of the app, which we currently expect to complete in the coming months.

During the period, Aave Labs’ UK subsidiaries Push Labs Limited and Push Virtual Assets Limited were registered with the Financial Conduct Authority as cryptoasset exchange providers under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017.

Aave Pro

Over the last 180 days, Aave Labs shipped a myriad of UI and UX improvements to Aave Pro on mobile and web.

The new markets page in Aave Pro brings each V4 market’s data, deposit and borrow assets, connected Hubs, and composition into a single view, and new reserve pages show each asset’s interest rates, supply and borrow caps, and top addresses. Watch wallets lets users track the V4 positions, balances, and activity of any wallet without connecting it, with custom names and avatars, and Merkl rewards lets users track and claim incentive rewards from Merkl, a rewards distribution platform, without leaving Aave Pro. With Avalanche support and the additions of Arc and Base, Aave Pro now covers every DAO-operated V4 deployment.

Aave Labs’ backend and full-stack engineers also rebuilt the system that indexes Aave V4 and serves its data to the Aave API and Aave Pro. The new backend consolidates protocol data into a single pipeline that is more robust, faster, and cheaper to run, and initial estimates show a 50x improvement on some of the heaviest load times in Aave Pro. Aave Labs started with V4 and will begin moving every protocol version and other data sources onto the same pipeline, which will let the team ship new features faster and give integrators confidence that the data they display is accurate.

The Earn and Borrow flows in Aave Pro were also rebuilt in Q3, which give users a clearer path to deposit, earn, and borrow across Aave V4 markets, and the new Earn flow replaced the Deposit page in October. The team also spent Q3 working on the functionality behind position swaps, which let users swap their collateral or debt from one asset to another without unwinding and reopening the position. Position swaps are expected to launch in Q4. Aave Labs is also developing a leverage feature for Aave Pro, which would let users open a leveraged position in a single flow instead of looping deposits and borrows by hand, and it is also expected to launch in Q4.

Aave V3 Interface

In July, the Staked GHO to Savings GHO migration tool went live so that stkGHO holders could move into Savings GHO in one step and keep earning at the Aave Savings Rate. In September, Aave Labs released a full redesign of the Aave V3 interface to bring the UI/UX to a standard expected from Aave products. This was followed by asset swaps and position swaps powered by CoW Swap on the Plasma market, which let users swap any asset, or swap their collateral and debt, with protection against front-running.

Aave Kit

Stable Vaults launched in July as the vault infrastructure behind Aave App, with per-user earning rates, earning across multiple chains and strategies, and deposits and withdrawals in multiple stablecoins. Any business can use Stable Vaults to embed onchain stablecoin yield in its own product, choosing which stablecoins to accept, which strategies to run, and what rate to offer each user, without building the underlying infrastructure itself. Certora formally verified the Stable Vault, Funds Handler, Asset Registry, Allocator, and IOU token contracts.

Aave Labs released the official Aave MCP server in September. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the standard AI assistants use to connect to outside tools, and the Aave MCP server gives those assistants one endpoint to read protocol data, manage positions, and prepare transactions across every Aave V3 and V4 deployment, with no authentication, API key, or signup required. The server never holds user funds and returns unsigned transactions for the user’s own wallet to approve.

Aave Labs’ design engineering team developed the refraction technique behind Aave Glass for the web, along with the family of interface components that use it. The technique works in Chromium, Safari, and Firefox on desktop and mobile, and Aave Labs published a write-up that covers the displacement map, the WebGL path for canvas and video surfaces, and other implementation details.

Aave Institutional

Aave Labs spent Q2 and Q3 building out new institutional pipelines including a new credit offering designed to bring institutional users to Aave, and brought the Aave Institutional ARFC to Snapshot on September 30. A governance proposal published on September 15 also introduced Custodied Collateral Lending on V4, which would let institutions borrow stablecoins against assets held in custody at Anchorage, with balances kept in sync onchain through Chainlink CustodySync. Together, these initiatives are intended to open Aave to institutional users it has not previously reached.

In June, Bitwise became the investment manager of USCC on Aave Horizon, which already held over $120 million USCC deposits, and Midas’s mGLOBAL went live on June 23 with a strategy managed by Fasanara Capital. Active loans backed by real-world assets on Aave Horizon and other Aave markets passed $500 million on June 30.

Securitize also proposed onboarding HINC, the Neuberger Securitize High Income Tokenized Fund, to Aave Horizon, and Midas proposed onboarding mWIN, a fixed income strategy managed by Wellington Management. In September, Aave Labs also announced V4’s first RWA Hub on Avalanche, which is expected to use Tether’s USA₮ as its main source of dollar liquidity, and work on the Hub is underway ahead of launch.

Security and Infrastructure

Throughout Q2 and Q3, Aave Labs built out a dedicated smart contract security team, which now sits under the new Chief Information Security Officer role, and scoped, scheduled, and managed more than 20 security engagements across the protocol and product stack.

On April 10, Aave Labs completed a SOC 2 Type II examination covering the Trust Services Criteria of Security, Availability, and Confidentiality, an independent assessment of the controls Aave Labs uses to develop and operate its software.

The bug bounty restructure went live on May 14, which aligned payouts with the risk level of each part of the Aave ecosystem, simplified the review process, and raised the payout caps for critical bugs fivefold on Aave V4 and Core Aave V3. Aave’s bug bounties now run on Immunefi, Sherlock, and Cantina, with ongoing triage of submitted reports.

On August 13, Aave Labs published the first results from AI-assisted security scanning of V3 and V4, which adds automated review alongside the human audits that have covered every Aave protocol generation since 2020.

Aave Labs also published the Technical Asset Listing Framework on May 28, which sets one technical standard for every new asset listing, continued listing, and material parameter change across Aave V3, Aave V4, and Aave Horizon.

Aave Labs also supported LlamaRisk’s initiative to derisk low-value assets on Aave V3 by implementing the payloads for AIP 521, which deprecated low-adoption assets, and AIP 526, which deprecated the oracles for long-tail assets.

Throughout Q2-Q3, Aave Labs published technical network assessments ahead of each new deployment. Aave Labs also implemented the payload that funded Certora’s Concord Equivalence Checker, a tool that confirms upgraded contracts behave the same as the code they replace, and in August it led the rotation of signers on the Aave Governance Emergency Guardian, the multisig that can cancel malicious governance proposals.

Aave Labs also supported the setup of emergency multisigs for V4 and Aave Horizon, strengthened device and identity security across the team in response to industry-wide phishing activity, ran disaster recovery and key-holder readiness exercises, and published a new security page at aave.com/security.

Lastly, Aave Labs built Aave Checkpoint, which is a tool that checks governance proposal code against its forum specification before execution.

Q4 Outlook

Q4 started out strong with the launch of the first externally curated markets on Aave V4, as Sentora deployed its own Liquidity Hub on Ethereum on October 22. Aave Pro added a new Earn flow along with support for externally curated Hubs, Ethena Pay launched Earn+ with a vault strategy that runs on Aave V4 on Avalanche, and active loans on V4 passed $500 million for the first time.

Over the rest of the quarter, Aave Labs intends to support bringing V4 to more networks and assets, subject to governance approval. Proposals to deploy on Tempo and Monad are moving forward, native Bitcoin borrowing through Babylon is expected to follow once its audits are complete, and stock-backed loans on Base are expected to move to Chainlink 24/7 pricing, which keeps tokenized stock collateral priced through weekends and market holidays. Work on a number of other ongoing projects and partner integrations is also underway.

In parallel, Aave Labs is preparing to launch V4’s first RWA Hub on Avalanche, with Tether’s USA₮ as its main source of dollar liquidity. Aave Labs is also working toward making Custodied Collateral Lending and the Aave Institutional credit offerings operational, subject to governance approval where required.

Aave Labs also expects to bring the Aave App to Android and add more deposit chains, and to expand Aave Pro’s feature set with leverage, position swaps, and more. Aave Labs also plans to move the remaining protocol versions onto its rebuilt data pipeline and continue laying the groundwork for Phase 1 of the Aave Foundation, and we look forward to sharing that progress with the DAO in our next quarterly update. Plans described in this section reflect current expectations and may change.

Summary

Aave governance approved the Aave Will Win Framework in April 2026, and as part of that framework Aave Labs committed to publishing quarterly updates on its work as a service provider to the Aave DAO. This report combines the first the 180 days since that approval, spanning Q2 and Q3 2026.

Over the last 180 days, Aave Labs’ team of about 97 team members put an estimated 100,000 hours into its work for the Aave DAO and completed 6,096 tracked issues and 36 projects of various scopes across engineering, security, product, design, growth, marketing, governance, and legal. Over the same period, Aave Labs authored 26 onchain governance proposals and 20 Snapshot votes, and shipped 28 items including products, features, and protocol deployments. Aave Labs also prepared and implemented the DAO-approved onboarding of 33 unique assets, deployments on four new chains, and four new Aave V4 Liquidity Hubs with their corresponding Spokes.

Throughout Q2, Aave Labs assumed roughly 40 technical and supporting functions that BGD Labs and the Aave Chan Initiative (ACI) previously performed for the DAO, including contract maintenance, security coordination, proposal payload engineering, and developer tooling, and it completed both transitions while rsETH incident response (detailed below) was still underway.

Q3 was a strong quarter for launches and product expansion across the Aave ecosystem. Following DAO approval, Aave Labs implemented Aave V4 deployments on Avalanche, Arc, and Base, and V4 grew from $212.6 million deposits to $1.34 billion in Q3, passing its first $1 billion on September 16. Since launching from zero at the end of March, V4 has grown to more than $1.3 billion deposits in roughly six months. Aave App opened early access on iOS, expanded to five total chains, and launched instant onramps for eligible U.S. users through licensed third-party providers. We also opened up Stable Vaults, the vault infrastructure behind the Aave App, for enterprise use. Other key launches include the official Aave MCP server, which gives AI a direct connection to read Aave data and prepare transactions, the Aave V3 interface redesign, and the addition of each new V4 deployment to Aave Pro.

On the security side, Certora completed formal verification of core Aave V4 and Stable Vaults contracts against defined specifications, and three new V4 security audits were published over the period. Aave Labs coordinated these engagements, including scoping, remediation of findings, and fix review, before the final reports were published.

Aave Labs’ UK subsidiaries Push Labs Limited and Push Virtual Assets Limited (together, Push) were also registered with the Financial Conduct Authority as cryptoasset exchange providers. Push provides fiat on- and off-ramp services for eligible Aave App users.

Aave protocol revenue totaled $44.58 million across the 180 days, while deposits across all versions of the protocol grew by $9.69 billion in Q3 alone.
