rsETH Response

On April 18 at 17:35 UTC, an exploit of the rsETH cross-chain bridge resulted in the release of 116,500 rsETH on Ethereum without a matching amount being burned on the source chain. The exploit did not involve the Aave Protocol’s smart contracts, which continued to operate as designed. The attacker supplied 89,567 of the stolen rsETH across eight Aave V3 positions and borrowed 82,650 WETH and 821 wstETH against it, after which the Aave Protocol Guardian froze the affected reserves within 85 minutes and the Risk Stewards made roughly 295 parameter changes across V3 reserves over the following weeks to contain exposure.

Aave Labs, TokenLogic, and LlamaRisk then helped coordinate DeFi United, a cross-protocol effort to restore rsETH’s backing for affected users. Within a week, Consensys and Joseph Lubin committed up to 30,000 ETH with strategic advice from SharpLink, Aave service providers proposed that Aave DAO contribute 25,000 ETH, and Golem contributed 1,000 ETH, while EtherFi, Ethena, Mantle, Frax, the Ink Foundation, Tydro, and LayerZero also joined the effort.

On April 25, Aave service providers, together with EtherFi, Kelp, LayerZero, Compound, and others, submitted a proposal asking the Arbitrum DAO to release into the recovery the ETH that the Arbitrum Security Council had frozen after the exploit. The vote reached quorum with more than 1,600 addresses representing over 190 million ARB. On May 1, a restraining notice was issued against the Arbitrum DAO in connection with an unrelated case. Following an application by Aave LLC, the court modified the notice on May 8 to allow the onchain vote and the transfer of the ETH to Aave LLC.

Aave governance executed AIP 478 on May 6, which liquidated the eight attacker positions without affecting any other users or Umbrella, Aave’s staking-based backstop. AIP 482 followed on May 16 and restored WETH borrowing limits to their pre-incident levels across the V3 Ethereum Core, Ethereum Prime, Arbitrum, Base, Mantle, and Linea markets. Kelp refilled the bridge with recovered rsETH across five tranches totaling 116,131.72 rsETH, which fully restored rsETH’s backing by May 26 and returned all Aave markets to normal operation.

Aave Labs prioritized its incident response work over its launch schedule and moved the affected launches into Q3. The public post mortem gives a fuller account of the response.

DAO Launches Overview

Aave Labs authored 26 onchain proposals and 20 Snapshot votes over the 180 days, and it submitted another 16 onchain proposals on behalf of other service providers. Onchain proposals are binding votes that execute code on the protocol, and Snapshot votes are offchain votes the DAO uses to approve a direction before the onchain step.

Aave Labs submitted the other 16 proposals in collaboration with TokenLogic, LlamaRisk, Chaos Labs, and Certora as part of the payload engineering function it took over from BGD Labs. A payload is the smart contract code that a proposal executes, and Aave Labs now writes, tests, and submits that code for other service providers in addition to its own proposals.

Aave Labs also published the Technical Asset Listing Framework to the governance forum on May 28, which sets one technical standard for every new asset listing, continued listing, and material parameter expansion across Aave V3, Aave V4, and Aave Horizon, along with requirements for ongoing monitoring of listed assets. The framework passed Snapshot in July and is now a formal part of the asset onboarding process.

Assets Onboarded

Eight came through standalone listing proposals, and 25 launched with the four new chain deployments. Functions Absorbed from BGD Labs and ACI

During Q2, Aave Labs assumed roughly 40 technical and supporting functions from BGD Labs and ACI (with others taken on by TokenLogic), spanning developer tooling, security coordination, and governance infrastructure. Aave Labs now maintains the Aave Address Book, which is the official registry of every Aave contract address and deployment, the Aave Helpers, which are shared code libraries used across proposals, the Aave CLI, which is the command-line toolkit developers use to build on Aave, and the Aave Permission Book, which publicly documents the addresses that hold permissions on the protocol.

Aave Labs is also adapting the Correlated Assets Price Oracle (CAPO) to V4. CAPO limits how quickly the price of a yield-bearing asset such as wstETH can rise, which protects Aave markets from price manipulation.

Through the same transition, Aave Labs took on security coordination and vulnerability response support for V3 and earlier versions, along with ongoing contract maintenance for those versions and the deprecation of the legacy Safety Module. Aave Labs now prepares the technical deployment work for DAO-approved asset listings and chain launches across protocol versions, which over this period included the V3 Monad market and the V4 Avalanche, Arc, and Base deployments.

Aave V4

Aave V4 passed $1 billion deposits on September 16 and reached a high of $1.41 billion on October 12. Over the 180 days, V4 expanded from Ethereum to three more chains, with four new Liquidity Hubs and seven new markets approved by the DAO and implemented by Aave Labs, while deposits grew in every month of the period and active loans passed $400 million on September 29.

The Global Dollar Hub went live on Ethereum on July 1 as the first new Liquidity Hub since V4 launched, and it is built for assets tied to Paxos’ USDG stablecoin. Maple’s syrupUSDG and Paxos’ gold-backed PAXG joined the Hub in Q3, and USDG deposits on Aave passed $100 million in August.

Aave V4 went live on Avalanche on July 15, which made it the first V4 deployment outside Ethereum, and the deployment passed $30 million deposits on September 23. On September 16, Aave Labs announced that V4’s first RWA Hub, a market where institutions can borrow against tokenized real-world assets, is planned to launch on Avalanche, subject to governance approval, with Tether’s USA₮ as its main source of dollar liquidity.

Aave V4 went live on Arc, the layer 1 blockchain built by Circle, on September 16, the same day the network launched. The deployment passed $300 million deposits on October 12, and Maple’s syrupUSDC was added as collateral on October 7.

Aave V4 went live on Base on September 25 with the Equities Hub, which accepts Coinbase Tokenized Stocks as collateral. Access is limited to users in eligible jurisdictions outside the U.S.

Externally Managed V4 Instances

Two partners moved to run their own V4 instances during Q3, with each partner managing its instance outside the Aave DAO’s risk mandate and sharing revenue with Aave DAO.

On August 14, EtherFi moved the credit backend for EtherFi Cash to a dedicated Aave V4 instance on Optimism, which lets more than 100,000 cardholders borrow against PAXG, SPYx, WBTC, ETH, and ETHFI. The instance passed $100 million deposits in its first week. EtherFi manages the instance itself, outside Aave DAO governance, and it shares a portion of its revenue with Aave DAO.

Sentora published an ARFC on September 28 for an externally curated Hub and Spoke framework on V4, under which Sentora would run its own Liquidity Hub on Ethereum with RLUSD Yield, OUSD Yield, and Bluechip markets at launch and a PYUSD Yield market planned later. Sentora sets collateral, risk parameters, interest rate curves, liquidation settings, and oracles, while the Aave DAO Governance Short Executor keeps ownership of the contracts and admin roles, and any change that increases risk would wait 48 hours behind an onchain timelock. Aave DAO receives 50 percent of the instance’s protocol revenue.

Babylon Integration

Native BTC loans, powered by Babylon’s Trustless Vaults, ran on V4 testnet in June, and the integration is now in audit with Certora, two independent researchers, and an internal Aave Labs review. Bringing native Bitcoin to V4 would unlock much more BTC collateral for Aave than currently exists inside the wrapped versions of the asset.

V4-Specific Security and Risk Management

Aave Labs’ smart contract security team led the security work on V4 over the 180 days. Alongside external audits, the team introduced AI-assisted code review across Aave Labs repositories and coordinated each external engagement through scoping, remediation, and fix review.

Aave Labs worked with Certora to formally verify the core V4 contracts in July, covering the Liquidity Hub, the Spoke, and the Tokenization Spoke contracts along with the math libraries they rely on. Formal verification uses mathematical proofs to check that code behaves according to a defined set of specifications. Aave Labs also worked with Sherlock on a new V4 security audit published May 26, and with ChainSecurity on two more, one on the Tokenization Spoke published June 19 and one on the Liquidity Hub, Spoke, and position manager contracts published July 21.

AIP 523, authored by Aave Labs and approved by the DAO, activated Risk Stewards on V4 on September 25. Risk Stewards allow risk service providers to raise or lower supply caps, borrow caps, and other risk settings within preset limits and waiting periods, so V4 can adjust to demand within days, with no separate DAO vote needed for each change.

Aave Labs also worked to integrate Chainlink SVR into Aave V4 markets for eligible assets. SVR, short for Smart Value Recapture, captures the profit that bots earn from liquidations and returns it to the DAO, and on V3 it has returned over $11 million to the DAO treasury since March 2025.

Product Overview

Over the 180 days covered in this report, Aave product surface area expanded significantly, including a consumer app for earning onchain stablecoin yield, enterprise vault infrastructure, a direct connection for AI agents, and a redesigned V3 app. Aave Labs shipped several items including products, features, and protocol deployments over the 180 days.

Aave App

Aave App opened to its first users through Ghost Passes on August 26, and since then users from around the world have started using the app, funding it with stablecoins or from their bank accounts through Push and licensed providers. Balances across all Aave App users have since crossed $45 million.

During Q3, Aave Labs added instant deposit onboarding for eligible U.S. users, provided through licensed providers, and expanded Aave App from one chain to five, adding Ethereum, Base, HyperEVM, and BNB Chain to Arbitrum so users can deposit stablecoins from any of those networks. Aave Labs also spent Q3 developing the Android version of the app, which we currently expect to complete in the coming months.

During the period, Aave Labs’ UK subsidiaries Push Labs Limited and Push Virtual Assets Limited were registered with the Financial Conduct Authority as cryptoasset exchange providers under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017.

Aave Pro

Over the last 180 days, Aave Labs shipped a myriad of UI and UX improvements to Aave Pro on mobile and web.

The new markets page in Aave Pro brings each V4 market’s data, deposit and borrow assets, connected Hubs, and composition into a single view, and new reserve pages show each asset’s interest rates, supply and borrow caps, and top addresses. Watch wallets lets users track the V4 positions, balances, and activity of any wallet without connecting it, with custom names and avatars, and Merkl rewards lets users track and claim incentive rewards from Merkl, a rewards distribution platform, without leaving Aave Pro. With Avalanche support and the additions of Arc and Base, Aave Pro now covers every DAO-operated V4 deployment.

Aave Labs’ backend and full-stack engineers also rebuilt the system that indexes Aave V4 and serves its data to the Aave API and Aave Pro. The new backend consolidates protocol data into a single pipeline that is more robust, faster, and cheaper to run, and initial estimates show a 50x improvement on some of the heaviest load times in Aave Pro. Aave Labs started with V4 and will begin moving every protocol version and other data sources onto the same pipeline, which will let the team ship new features faster and give integrators confidence that the data they display is accurate.

The Earn and Borrow flows in Aave Pro were also rebuilt in Q3, which give users a clearer path to deposit, earn, and borrow across Aave V4 markets, and the new Earn flow replaced the Deposit page in October. The team also spent Q3 working on the functionality behind position swaps, which let users swap their collateral or debt from one asset to another without unwinding and reopening the position. Position swaps are expected to launch in Q4. Aave Labs is also developing a leverage feature for Aave Pro, which would let users open a leveraged position in a single flow instead of looping deposits and borrows by hand, and it is also expected to launch in Q4.

Aave V3 Interface

In July, the Staked GHO to Savings GHO migration tool went live so that stkGHO holders could move into Savings GHO in one step and keep earning at the Aave Savings Rate. In September, Aave Labs released a full redesign of the Aave V3 interface to bring the UI/UX to a standard expected from Aave products. This was followed by asset swaps and position swaps powered by CoW Swap on the Plasma market, which let users swap any asset, or swap their collateral and debt, with protection against front-running.

Aave Kit

Stable Vaults launched in July as the vault infrastructure behind Aave App, with per-user earning rates, earning across multiple chains and strategies, and deposits and withdrawals in multiple stablecoins. Any business can use Stable Vaults to embed onchain stablecoin yield in its own product, choosing which stablecoins to accept, which strategies to run, and what rate to offer each user, without building the underlying infrastructure itself. Certora formally verified the Stable Vault, Funds Handler, Asset Registry, Allocator, and IOU token contracts.

Aave Labs released the official Aave MCP server in September. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the standard AI assistants use to connect to outside tools, and the Aave MCP server gives those assistants one endpoint to read protocol data, manage positions, and prepare transactions across every Aave V3 and V4 deployment, with no authentication, API key, or signup required. The server never holds user funds and returns unsigned transactions for the user’s own wallet to approve.

Aave Labs’ design engineering team developed the refraction technique behind Aave Glass for the web, along with the family of interface components that use it. The technique works in Chromium, Safari, and Firefox on desktop and mobile, and Aave Labs published a write-up that covers the displacement map, the WebGL path for canvas and video surfaces, and other implementation details.

Aave Institutional

Aave Labs spent Q2 and Q3 building out new institutional pipelines including a new credit offering designed to bring institutional users to Aave, and brought the Aave Institutional ARFC to Snapshot on September 30. A governance proposal published on September 15 also introduced Custodied Collateral Lending on V4, which would let institutions borrow stablecoins against assets held in custody at Anchorage, with balances kept in sync onchain through Chainlink CustodySync. Together, these initiatives are intended to open Aave to institutional users it has not previously reached.

In June, Bitwise became the investment manager of USCC on Aave Horizon, which already held over $120 million USCC deposits, and Midas’s mGLOBAL went live on June 23 with a strategy managed by Fasanara Capital. Active loans backed by real-world assets on Aave Horizon and other Aave markets passed $500 million on June 30.

Securitize also proposed onboarding HINC, the Neuberger Securitize High Income Tokenized Fund, to Aave Horizon, and Midas proposed onboarding mWIN, a fixed income strategy managed by Wellington Management. In September, Aave Labs also announced V4’s first RWA Hub on Avalanche, which is expected to use Tether’s USA₮ as its main source of dollar liquidity, and work on the Hub is underway ahead of launch.

Security and Infrastructure

Throughout Q2 and Q3, Aave Labs built out a dedicated smart contract security team, which now sits under the new Chief Information Security Officer role, and scoped, scheduled, and managed more than 20 security engagements across the protocol and product stack.

On April 10, Aave Labs completed a SOC 2 Type II examination covering the Trust Services Criteria of Security, Availability, and Confidentiality, an independent assessment of the controls Aave Labs uses to develop and operate its software.

The bug bounty restructure went live on May 14, which aligned payouts with the risk level of each part of the Aave ecosystem, simplified the review process, and raised the payout caps for critical bugs fivefold on Aave V4 and Core Aave V3. Aave’s bug bounties now run on Immunefi, Sherlock, and Cantina, with ongoing triage of submitted reports.

On August 13, Aave Labs published the first results from AI-assisted security scanning of V3 and V4, which adds automated review alongside the human audits that have covered every Aave protocol generation since 2020.

Aave Labs also published the Technical Asset Listing Framework on May 28, which sets one technical standard for every new asset listing, continued listing, and material parameter change across Aave V3, Aave V4, and Aave Horizon.

Aave Labs also supported LlamaRisk’s initiative to derisk low-value assets on Aave V3 by implementing the payloads for AIP 521, which deprecated low-adoption assets, and AIP 526, which deprecated the oracles for long-tail assets.

Throughout Q2-Q3, Aave Labs published technical network assessments ahead of each new deployment. Aave Labs also implemented the payload that funded Certora’s Concord Equivalence Checker, a tool that confirms upgraded contracts behave the same as the code they replace, and in August it led the rotation of signers on the Aave Governance Emergency Guardian, the multisig that can cancel malicious governance proposals.

Aave Labs also supported the setup of emergency multisigs for V4 and Aave Horizon, strengthened device and identity security across the team in response to industry-wide phishing activity, ran disaster recovery and key-holder readiness exercises, and published a new security page at aave.com/security.

Lastly, Aave Labs built Aave Checkpoint, which is a tool that checks governance proposal code against its forum specification before execution.

Over the rest of the quarter, Aave Labs intends to support bringing V4 to more networks and assets, subject to governance approval. Proposals to deploy on Tempo and Monad are moving forward, native Bitcoin borrowing through Babylon is expected to follow once its audits are complete, and stock-backed loans on Base are expected to move to Chainlink 24/7 pricing, which keeps tokenized stock collateral priced through weekends and market holidays. governance_posts.description:
title: [Direct-to-AIP] Ethena E-Mode Consolidation on Aave V3
author: @TokenLogic
created: 2026-11-13

Summary

This publication proposes a common set of reference e-modes for Ethena collateral on Aave V3 Core, Plasma, Mantle, Monad and Avalanche. The proposed parameters are 91% LTV and 93% LT for USDe against stablecoins, and 90% LTV and 92% LT for sUSDe against stablecoins.

Legacy collateral on Core and Plasma would be retired through per-asset LTV-zero flags while keeping existing LTs, except Plasma #21, whose LT returns from 93.1% to 93%, and Plasma #23, which is aligned to the sUSDe reference parameters. The proposal also retires the matured PTs on Monad and in X Layer #7 and #8, and removes USDe borrowing from Avalanche #4.

Motivation

Overview

Several legacy Ethena PT e-modes continue to accept USDe or sUSDe after their PTs have matured. Their parameters and borrowable assets differ from the reference e-modes, so users with similar collateral can face different parameters and abuse Aave risk settings. Across Core #10, #29 and #34 and Plasma #13 and #21, legacy USDe e-modes account for approximately $709M of collateral and $637M of debt. Most of these categories offer 91% LTV, while Plasma #21 offers 91.1%, compared with 90% in the existing USDe reference modes on both markets. A common reference configuration would reduce the number of categories used for these positions.

USDe and sUSDe Deposits

Figures at the November 10, 2026 snapshot (Core block 26,387,055, Plasma block 37,400,956) cover all wallets with USDe or sUSDe enabled as collateral in the listed categories. Debt is those wallets’ total debt, including debt supported by other collateral.

Legacy Collateral and Existing Positions

Per-asset LTV-zero flags stop legacy collateral from supporting new borrowing while each category keeps its LT, so existing health factors are unchanged, and no position is hurt, except for the Plasma #21 and #23 changes below. A position borrowing USDC, USDT or USDT0 that wants to keep borrowing moves to the reference e-mode in a single transaction; USDe and USDtb debt is not permitted there.

Plasma #23 moves from 90.1% / 92.1% to 90% / 92%, in line with the sUSDe reference mode Plasma #2. This lowers health factors by about 0.001 and liquidates no positions at the snapshot.

The LT of legacy Plasma #21 returns from 93.1% to 93%, in line with reference mode Plasma #1 and the other legacy USDe categories. The lowest resulting health factor at the snapshot is 1.008, so no position is liquidated.

USDe Denominated Borrowing

The retirement list includes Core and Plasma categories that permit USDe borrowing against USDe, sUSDe or their matured PTs, with LTs of up to 96%. USDe is also removed from the borrowable assets of Avalanche #4, where about $1.4k of USDe is borrowed in total.

Specification

Part A: Reference E-Mode Parameters

The following updates apply to the existing reference categories. Liquidation bonuses, collateral membership, borrowable assets, and isolation flags remain unchanged in these categories, except that USDe is removed from Avalanche #4’s borrowable assets.

Core #2, Plasma #2, Mantle #1 and Monad #2 already provide 90% LTV and 92% LT for their sUSDe reference configurations and require no parameter changes. Plasma #23 moves from 90.1% / 92.1% to 90% / 92% to match Plasma #2, with its liquidation bonus unchanged; its sUSDe retirement is specified in Part B. Plasma #21’s LT moves from 93.1% to 93%, with its LTV and liquidation bonus unchanged; this can be executed in the AIP or by the Risk Stewards after it.

New Monad USDe reference e-mode

Monad’s existing #2 combines USDe and sUSDe at 90% LTV and 92% LT. A separate USDe reference category is proposed with the following configuration:

The borrowable set matches Monad #2. The liquidation bonus and isolation setting match the USDe reference modes on Core #11, Plasma #1, Mantle #2 and Avalanche #3.

Part B: Legacy Collateral Retirement

Each entry below sets the named asset’s per-asset LTV-zero flag to true in the listed categories. Membership and isolation are unchanged, and category parameters are unchanged except for Plasma #21 and #23 (Part A).

The two October PTs matured at 00:00 UTC on the 22nd of October. Their flags apply to both the stablecoin-debt and USDe-debt categories. Existing LTV-zero flags on older collateral remain in place. All listed collateral is already flagged LTV zero in Core #9, #13, #14, #15, #18, #25, #27 and #28, and Plasma #5, #6, #7 and #8, so these categories require no additional flag change at the snapshot configuration.

Each change is a setAssetLtvzeroInEMode(asset, categoryId, true) call, checked against the configuration at execution.

Part C: Other Legacy Collateral

Part C retires all listed collateral in Monad #5 and X Layer #7 and #8. X Layer #9 is left unchanged so October PT positions can roll into the February PT, and its October PT is flagged by the next USDG rollover. Together, Parts B and C specify 38 per-asset LTV-zero flag changes.

Future PT rollovers

To keep this from building up again, we propose that each future PT rollover payload will also set LTV zero on every PT that has matured by the time it executes, in all e-modes where it is collateral. Once every PT in an e-mode has matured, the same payload flags the spot asset in that e-mode. Liquidation thresholds stay unchanged. PTs are flagged only after maturity, so no user has to sell a PT before it redeems at par.

Disclaimer

TokenLogic is an active service provider to the Aave DAO, the beneficiary of stream 100086 and the KPI as outlined in this publication. The scope of this engagement is available via this forum proposal.

TokenLogic supports and maintains an independent delegate voting platform within the Aave community.

TokenLogic and associated entities have no undisclosed material conflicts of interest at the time of submission.

Next Steps

  1. Gather feedback from the community.
  2. Escalate this proposal to the AIP stage.

governance_posts.title: Risk Stewards: Supply and Borrow Cap Changes on Aave V3 / 2026.11.13
governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

Aave V3 Core:

  • Increase supply cap for cbBTC from 20,000 to 22,500.
  • Reduce supply cap for weETH from 1,500,000 to 1,420,000.
  • Reduce supply cap for WBTC from 38,200 to 35,500.
  • Reduce supply cap for BTC.b from 225 to 40.
  • Reduce supply cap for eBTC from 134 to 100.

Aave V3 Mantle:

  • Reduce supply cap for USDT0 from 312,500,000 to 150,000,000.
  • Reduce borrow cap for USDT0 from 152,000,000 to 125,000,000.
  • Reduce supply cap for sUSDe from 100,000,000 to 65,000,000.
  • Reduce supply cap for USDe from 80,000,000 to 50,000,000.

cbBTC (Aave V3 Core)

cbBTC has reached 97.2% supply cap utilization on the Aave V3 Core instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 13, 2026

All of the top 20 cbBTC suppliers carry debt, with health factors between 1.11 and 3.07 and a median of 1.60, and supply is concentrated, with the largest supplier at about 27% and the top 5 at about 72%. 16 of the 20 borrow USDC and 5 borrow USDT against cbBTC collateral, so HF in the cohort tracks mainly the BTC price.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 20,000 to 22,500 on Aave V3 Core, which places the reserve at approximately 86.4% post-change supply cap utilization.

Cap Reductions

  • weETH on Aave V3 Core sits at 90.5% supply cap utilization (1.36M / 1.5M), with supply down 1.6% over the past 30 days. The proposed cap of 1.42M lands at approximately 95.6% post-change cap utilization.
  • WBTC on Aave V3 Core sits at 90.1% supply cap utilization (34,432 / 38,200), with supply broadly unchanged over the past 30 days. The proposed cap of 35,500 lands at approximately 97.0% post-change cap utilization.
  • BTC.b on Aave V3 Core sits at 10.0% supply cap utilization (22.5 / 225), with supply up 47.6% over the past 30 days. The proposed cap of 40 lands at approximately 56.4% post-change cap utilization.
  • eBTC on Aave V3 Core sits at 54.1% supply cap utilization (72.5 / 134), with supply down 3.3% over the past 30 days. The proposed cap of 100 lands at approximately 72.5% post-change cap utilization.
  • USDT0 on Aave V3 Mantle sits at 32.8% supply cap utilization (102.43M / 312.5M) and 59.0% borrow cap utilization (89.66M / 152M), with supply down 35.9% and borrows down 36.5% over the past 30 days. The proposed caps of 150M supply and 125M borrow land at approximately 68.3% and 71.7% post-change cap utilization.
  • sUSDe on Aave V3 Mantle sits at 26.3% supply cap utilization (26.27M / 100M), with supply down 59.7% over the past 30 days. The proposed cap of 65M lands at approximately 40.4% post-change cap utilization.
  • USDe on Aave V3 Mantle sits at 23.9% supply cap utilization (19.1M / 80M), with supply down 30.6% over the past 30 days. The proposed cap of 50M lands at approximately 38.2% post-change cap utilization.

Specification

Supply Caps

Instance Asset Current Supply Cap Recommended Supply Cap
Aave V3 Core cbBTC 20,000 22,500
Aave V3 Core weETH 1,500,000 1,420,000
Aave V3 Core WBTC 38,200 35,500
Aave V3 Core BTC.b 225 40
Aave V3 Core eBTC 134 100
Aave V3 Mantle USDT0 312,500,000 150,000,000
Aave V3 Mantle sUSDe 100,000,000 65,000,000
Aave V3 Mantle USDe 80,000,000 50,000,000

Borrow Caps

Aave V3 Mantle USDT0 152,000,000 125,000,000

Next Steps

We will move forward and implement these updates via the Risk Steward process. The implemented changes can be reviewed on the LlamaRisk Risk Stewards Dashboard.

Disclosure

This review was independently prepared by LlamaRisk, a DeFi risk service provider funded in part by the Aave DAO. LlamaRisk is not directly affiliated with the protocol(s) reviewed in this assessment and did not receive any compensation from the protocol(s) or their affiliated entities for this work.

governance_posts.title: Technical Maintenance Proposals
governance_posts.description:
Summary

This thread will be used for technical maintenance updates across Aave deployments, to keep maintenance activity visible, structured, and easy for the DAO to track. It covers maintenance updates from November 2026 onward and is open to any DAO Service Provider responsible for a maintenance item.

Context

The Aave ecosystem spans multiple products, versions, and networks. Maintenance tasks are periodically required to keep this infrastructure consistent, secure, and aligned with the approved architecture.

Maintenance updates prior to November 2026 are recorded in the previous maintenance thread, which established a clear and transparent format for this type of change. That thread remains the reference for historical updates. From November 2026 onward, maintenance updates will be posted here, so the DAO has a single place to review what is changing, why it is needed, and how execution is happening.

Scope

This thread is intended for updates that are technical, limited in scope, and not expected to create material community disagreement.

Examples include:

  • Price feed and oracle adapter updates, for example when a feed is deprecated or optimized by its provider.
  • Oracle changes required by the deprecation or migration of an asset.
  • Replacement of auxiliary contracts with improved versions that do not change user positions or existing interfaces.
  • Permission and access control alignment, including the removal of roles that are no longer required.
  • Consistency updates that reduce differences between Aave deployments, and other changes required to keep components aligned with the approved architecture.

Where a change should go through the normal governance process, such as new asset listings, risk parameter changes that materially affect users, budget approvals, or incentive programs, it will follow the applicable ARFC, Snapshot, or AIP route rather than being handled as a maintenance update here.

How updates will be presented

For each maintenance item, the DAO Service Provider responsible for it will post a standalone update in this thread, structured as Simple Summary, Motivation, and Specification. Each update will describe the affected components, the contracts and functions involved, the execution path, and the expected user impact.

Where the update requires an onchain governance proposal, the post will be shared before the AIP is created. Where the update is executed through an authorized operational multisig or Security Council path, the post will explain that execution path and why it applies. If timing or security constraints require execution before public disclosure, the update will be posted as soon as practical after execution.

As a baseline, maintenance updates will remain open for community review before execution or AIP creation when timing allows. If the DAO raises material concerns about an item, it will be moved into the applicable ARFC, Snapshot, or AIP process instead of continuing as a maintenance update.

Disclaimer

Aave Labs is sharing this update as a service provider to the Aave DAO, as part of its approved scope of work in support of DAO operations.

governance_posts.title: [Direct-to-AIP] November 2026 - Funding Update
governance_posts.description:
title: [Direct-to-AIP] November 2026 - Funding Update
author: @TokenLogic
created: 2026-11-13

Summary

This publication presents the November Funding Update, consisting of the following key activities:

  • Acquire GHO to support the runway;
  • Consolidate assets held on other networks onto Ethereum;
  • Expand the MainnetSwapSteward;
  • Deposit the ETH held by the Collector into Aave;
  • Recover Merkl rewards held by the GSMs on Plasma and Monad;
  • Bug bounty payment; and,
  • Create and update Allowances to support Operations.

Motivation

This publication addresses near-term operational requirements, consolidates asset holdings across networks, and expands the MainnetSwapSteward to support the runway.

The MainnetSwapSteward and Aave Finance Committee (AFC) will continue executing a rolling GHO acquisition strategy to maintain adequate runway and preserve sufficient budget to fund ongoing growth initiatives.

Asset Consolidation

The GHO held by the Collectors on Plasma, Monad, and Arbitrum, around 1.18M, will be bridged to Ethereum to support the runway. Idle assets on Mantle, Gnosis and Sonic are also to be bridged to Ethereum, where they can be managed by the PoolExposureSteward and MainnetSwapSteward.

Expand MainnetSwapSteward

The Collector holds around 1.3M of USDtb, USDG, EURC and sUSDe that the MainnetSwapSteward cannot currently swap. Adding these tokens enables them to be converted to GHO.

Collector ETH

The Collector holds around 121 ETH that is not earning yield. This publication wraps it into WETH and deposits it into the Core instance.

GSM Merkl Rewards

The GHO GSMs on Plasma and Monad have accrued Merkl rewards, 613k WXPL and 1.46M WMON. Once claimed, these rewards sit on the GSM contracts and can only be moved by governance. This publication transfers them to the AFC, where they will be sold.

Incentive Campaigns

The 350k USDC held on Ahab will fund incentives for specific campaigns supporting targeted growth.

Bug Bounty Payouts

This month’s funding update includes one 1,000 USDC bug bounty payment to a security researcher and the associated 100 USDC fee payment to Immunefi.

Update

The V4 Base USDC supply from the August/September Funding Update was funded with USDC held on the AFC and GHO borrowed on Ahab; the growth allowances were not drawn. The private credit pilots will use Ahab’s existing wETH collateral, as the aEthLidoWETH allowance was cancelled. 100k USDC was bridged to the Incentive Budget Safe on Arc.

Specification

Ethereum

Runway

Use the MainnetSwapSteward and the already-approved Allowances to acquire 2.7M GHO and deposit it into the Prime instance.

Bug Bounty Payments

The following bug bounty payments are to be processed to the researcher and Immunefi.

Asset: USDC 0xA0b86991c6218b36c1d19D4a2e9Eb0cE3606eB48
Amount: 1,000
Spender: Researcher 0x0DDE46b923eB74F1860727914f179e82b9eE47B9

Asset: USDC 0xA0b86991c6218b36c1d19D4a2e9Eb0cE3606eB48
Amount: 100
Spender: Immunefi 0x7119f398b6C06095c6E8964C1f58e7C1BAa79E18

Deposit ETH

Wrap the ETH held by the Collector into WETH and deposit it into the Core instance on the Collector’s behalf.

Asset: ETH, wrapped into WETH 0xC02aaA39b223FE8D0A0e5C4F27eAD9083C756Cc2
Amount: the Collector’s ETH balance at execution (120.86 at the time of writing)
Destination: Aave V3 Core, aEthWETH held by the Collector

Expand MainnetSwapSteward

Add the following tokens to the MainnetSwapSteward with GHO as the acquirable asset. Price feeds are to be confirmed with the payload implementer.

Allowances

Refresh the existing aEthLidoGHO Allowance to the Aave V4 audit Safe down to 250k.

Asset: aEthLidoGHO 0x18eFE565A5373f430e2F809b97De30335B3ad96A
Amount: 250k
Spender: Aave V4 audit Safe 0xAAf400e4Bbc38B5E2136C1a36946Bf841A357307

Cancel the following Allowance:

Asset: aEthGHO 0x00907f9921424583e7ffBfEdf84F92B7B2Be4977
Spender: Ahab 0xAA2461f0f0A3dE5fEAF3273eAe16DEF861cf594e

Plasma

Create a GHO Allowance for the AFC to bridge the GHO held on the Collector to Ethereum via CCIP.

Asset: GHO 0xb77E872A68C62CfC0dFb02C067Ecc3DA23B4bbf3
Amount: 1M
Spender: AFC 0x22740deBa78d5a0c24C58C740e3715ec29de1bFa

On the GHO USDT GSM 0xd06114F714beCD6f373e5cE94E07278eF46eBF37:

  1. Grant TOKEN_RESCUER_ROLE to the Plasma Executor Lvl 1 0x47aAdaAE1F05C978E6aBb7568d11B7F6e0FC4d6A.
  2. Call rescueTokens(WXPL, AFC, amount), with amount equal to the GSM’s WXPL balance at execution (613,220 at the time of writing). Recipient: AFC 0x22740deBa78d5a0c24C58C740e3715ec29de1bFa.
  3. Revoke TOKEN_RESCUER_ROLE from the Plasma Executor.

Monad

Create a GHO Allowance for the AFC to bridge the GHO held on the Collector to Ethereum via CCIP.

Asset: GHO 0xfc421aD3C883Bf9E7C4f42dE845C4e4405799e73
Amount: 250k
Spender: AFC 0x22740deBa78d5a0c24C58C740e3715ec29de1bFa

Prior to execution, the AFC will claim the Merkl rewards on behalf of the GHO USDC GSM 0x3Cf3779EEf770931543ACd2C7f6ECd1b37E35caB. On the GSM:

  1. Grant TOKEN_RESCUER_ROLE to the Monad Executor Lvl 1 0xa9d0EAFF48cE1DF468f9eAeb7e628c413343F6A2.
  2. Call rescueTokens(WMON, AFC, amount), with WMON 0x3bd359C1119dA7Da1D913D1C4D2B7c461115433A and amount equal to the GSM’s WMON balance at execution (1,458,970 accrued at the time of writing). Recipient: AFC 0x22740deBa78d5a0c24C58C740e3715ec29de1bFa.
  3. Revoke TOKEN_RESCUER_ROLE from the Monad Executor.

governance_posts.title: Temp Check / Discussion: Exploration of Aave Deployment on Cardano (Feasibility Study Proposal)
governance_posts.description:
Summary

This ARC proposes initiating a structured feasibility study to evaluate the potential deployment of Aave on Cardano.

The objective is to assess:

  • Technical compatibility

  • Risk framework requirements

  • Liquidity and market viability

This is the first step to determine whether further exploration is justified.

Motivation

Aave has successfully expanded across multiple EVM-compatible networks. However, the broader DeFi ecosystem remains concentrated around a single execution paradigm.

At the same time, alternative blockchain architectures have matured. Cardano represents one such environment, characterized by:

  • eUTXO-based transaction model

  • Functional programming approach to smart contracts

  • Emphasis on deterministic execution and formal methods

  • High levels of validator decentralization

Despite these properties, DeFi activity and TVL on Cardano remain relatively limited compared to other ecosystems.

This creates a potential opportunity to evaluate whether:

  • Aave could act as a foundational DeFi primitive in that environment

  • A new user and liquidity segment could be accessed

  • Architectural diversification could provide strategic value

Strategic Considerations

1. Architectural Diversification

Exploring deployment outside the EVM ecosystem may:

  • Reduce reliance on a single execution model

  • Provide exposure to alternative design trade-offs

2. Early Positioning in an Underdeveloped DeFi Market

Cardano currently lacks mature lending infrastructure at scale.
Aave could potentially:

  • Establish early presence

  • Define risk and collateral standards in a new environment

3. Emerging Collateral Opportunities (Forward-Looking)

There is ongoing development in the Cardano ecosystem around non-custodial Bitcoin interoperability, including approaches leveraging Zero-Knowledge technologies.

If successful, this could enable:

  • Use of BTC as collateral without custodial bridges

  • Reduced counterparty risk compared to wrapped assets

While early-stage, this direction may represent a differentiated collateral landscape worth monitoring.

Specification (Feasibility Study Scope)

This ARC proposes conducting a 6–8 week feasibility study covering:

Technical Assessment

  • Mapping Aave architecture to Cardano’s eUTXO model

  • Evaluation of smart contract design constraints

  • Identification of required adaptations or redesigns

Risk & Oracle Framework

  • Oracle availability and reliability

  • Liquidation mechanisms under eUTXO constraints

  • Risk parameter modeling

Market & Liquidity Analysis

  • Current DeFi activity and liquidity depth

  • Potential collateral assets

  • Incentive requirements for market bootstrapping

Ecosystem Dependencies

  • Required infrastructure (indexing, analytics, tooling)

  • Potential collaborators within the Cardano ecosystem

Implementation Considerations

Execution of the feasibility study could be carried out by:

  • Independent contributors

  • Ecosystem-aligned teams

  • External service providers

Subject to community alignment, a follow-up proposal (ARFC) would define:

  • Selected contributors

  • Detailed scope

  • Budget and timeline

Risks

Technical Complexity

  • Fundamental differences between account-based and eUTXO models

  • Potential need for partial or full redesign of components

Liquidity Fragmentation

  • Limited existing DeFi liquidity on Cardano

  • Dependence on incentives and ecosystem coordination

Opportunity Cost

  • Resource allocation vs. expanding within existing EVM ecosystems

Ecosystem Maturity

  • Tooling, oracle infrastructure, and integrations may require additional development

Cost & Funding

This ARC does not request funding.

If the community supports proceeding, a future ARFC would include:

  • A project submission on Project Catalyst to fund the initiative

Next Steps

This ARC seeks feedback from the community on:

  • Whether exploring a non-EVM deployment aligns with Aave’s strategy

  • Whether Cardano is a relevant ecosystem to evaluate

  • Whether the proposed feasibility study scope is appropriate

If there is sufficient support, the next step would be:
→ Drafting an ARFC with defined contributors, scope, and funding requirements.

Conclusion

This proposal does not advocate immediate deployment, but rather a structured evaluation of a potential strategic expansion.

The goal is to determine whether Cardano represents:

  • A viable new market for Aave

  • A meaningful diversification of execution environments

  • A forward-looking opportunity tied to emerging collateral models

Community feedback will determine whether further steps are warranted.

governance_posts.title: Risk Stewards: Supply and Borrow Cap Increases on Aave V3 / 2026.11.15
governance_posts.description:
Summary

LlamaRisk recommends the following parameter changes based on user behavior, on-chain liquidity, and position health observed in the latest review of Aave V3 reserves.

Aave V3 Core:

  • Increase supply cap for wstETH from 850,000 to 900,000.

Aave V3 Monad:

  • Increase supply cap for mUSD from 50,000,000 to 75,000,000.
  • Increase borrow cap for mUSD from 40,000,000 to 50,000,000.

Aave V3 Arbitrum:

  • Increase supply cap for AAVE from 10,400 to 20,000.

Aave V3 Gnosis:

  • Increase borrow cap for EURe from 10,600,000 to 12,000,000.

wstETH (Aave V3 Core)

wstETH has reached 98.9% supply cap utilization on the Aave V3 Core instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 15, 2026

19 of the top 20 wstETH suppliers carry debt, with health factors between 1.03 and 10.58 and a median of 1.92, and supply is moderately concentrated, with the largest supplier at about 14% and the top 5 at about 37%. 16 of the 20 borrow USDT and 9 borrow USDC, so HF for most of the cohort tracks the ETH price, while the 3 WETH borrowers hold the largest debt by value against ETH-correlated collateral.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 850,000 to 900,000 on Aave V3 Core, which places the reserve at approximately 93.4% post-change supply cap utilization.

mUSD (Aave V3 Monad)

mUSD has reached 99.8% supply cap utilization and 84.4% borrow cap utilization on the Aave V3 Monad instance. Supply is highly concentrated, with the largest supplier (mUSD Vault) holding about 99.8% of mUSD supplied.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 15, 2026

The top 20 mUSD borrowers run health factors between 1.00 and 1.12 with a median of 1.03, and the largest borrower accounts for about 34% of mUSD debt. 14 hold syrupUSDC and 6 hold PT-AUSD-17DEC2026 as collateral against stablecoin debt, so HF in the cohort depends on the exchange rate of these yield-bearing stablecoin collaterals against the borrowed stablecoins.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 50,000,000 to 75,000,000 and the borrow cap from 40,000,000 to 50,000,000 on Aave V3 Monad, which places the reserve at approximately 66.6% post-change supply cap utilization and 67.5% borrow cap utilization.

AAVE (Aave V3 Arbitrum)

AAVE has reached 100.0% supply cap utilization on the Aave V3 Arbitrum instance.

Supply Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 15, 2026

14 of the 17 largest AAVE suppliers carry debt, with health factors between 1.29 and 3.38 and a median of 2.00, and supply is dispersed, with the largest supplier at about 7% and the top 5 at about 24%. 11 borrow USDC and 3 borrow USD₮0, and several also hold WETH or WBTC alongside AAVE as collateral.

Liquidity

Users can swap 1.8K AAVE for $172K USDC within a price impact of 10%.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the supply cap from 10,400 to 20,000 ($2.1M) on Aave V3 Arbitrum, which places the reserve at approximately 52.0% post-change supply cap utilization.

EURe (Aave V3 Gnosis)

EURe has reached 96.7% borrow cap utilization on the Aave V3 Gnosis instance.

Borrow Distribution


Source: LlamaRisk, November 15, 2026

The top 20 EURe borrowers run health factors between 1.06 and 4.01 with a median of 1.29, and the largest borrower accounts for about 69% of EURe debt. 11 borrow against sDAI collateral, so their HF tracks the EUR/USD exchange rate, while the largest borrower holds wstETH and GNO collateral, so its HF tracks the ETH and GNO prices.

Recommendation

We recommend raising the borrow cap from 10,600,000 to 12,000,000 on Aave V3 Gnosis, which places the reserve at approximately 85.4% post-change borrow cap utilization.

Specification

Supply Caps

Instance Asset Current Supply Cap Recommended Supply Cap
Aave V3 Core wstETH 850,000 900,000
Aave V3 Monad mUSD 50,000,000 75,000,000
Aave V3 Arbitrum AAVE 10,400 20,000

Borrow Caps

Instance Asset Current Borrow Cap Recommended Borrow Cap
Aave V3 Monad mUSD 40,000,000 50,000,000
Aave V3 Gnosis EURe 10,600,000 12,000,000

Next Steps

We will move forward and implement these updates via the Risk Steward process. The implemented changes can be reviewed on the LlamaRisk Risk Stewards Dashboard.

Disclosure

This review was independently prepared by LlamaRisk, a DeFi risk service provider funded in part by the Aave DAO. LlamaRisk is not directly affiliated with the protocol(s) reviewed in this assessment and did not receive any compensation from the protocol(s) or their affiliated entities for this work.

The information provided should not be construed as legal, financial, tax, or professional advice.

governance_posts.title: Core Wallet on Avalanche V3 forces unnecessary Ethereum network switch
governance_posts.description:
I am posting this here because I could not find an existing issue describing this exact Core + Avalanche V3 connection behavior.

I am using Aave V3 on Avalanche exclusively, with the Core browser extension.

There appears to be an unnecessary network-switch requirement during wallet connection.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Open the Core browser extension.
  2. Set the active network to Avalanche C-Chain.
  3. Open app.aave.com.
  4. Select Avalanche Market V3.
  5. Confirm that the Aave interface is already displaying the Avalanche market.
  6. Select Connect Wallet → Core.
  7. During the connection process, Core displays:

“app.aave.com is requesting to switch your active network to Ethereum.”

  1. If I reject the Ethereum network switch, the Core/Aave wallet connection fails.
  2. If I approve the switch to Ethereum, the wallet connects successfully.
  3. When I later initiate an Aave transaction on Avalanche, I then have to switch the wallet back from Ethereum to Avalanche C-Chain.

Expected behavior

Because:

  • Aave is already set to Avalanche Market V3
  • Core is already connected to Avalanche C-Chain
  • all of my Aave activity is on Avalanche

the wallet connection should initialize directly on Avalanche C-Chain (chain ID 43114).

There should be no need to switch to Ethereum Mainnet during the initial connection and then switch back to Avalanche for the transaction.

Actual behavior

The current sequence is:

Core on Avalanche → Aave Avalanche V3 → Connect Core → forced Ethereum switch → wallet connects → initiate Avalanche transaction → switch back to Avalanche

Rejecting the Ethereum switch prevents the wallet from connecting.

Additional information

  • Wallet: Core browser extension
  • dApp: app.aave.com
  • Market: Aave V3 Avalanche
  • Intended network: Avalanche C-Chain
  • Ethereum transactions involved: None
  • ETH gas involved: None
  • Issue is reproducible consistently.

I have attached a screenshot showing Aave already on the Avalanche V3 market while Core simultaneously reports that app.aave.com is requesting a switch to Ethereum.

Could you please confirm whether this Ethereum-first connection behavior is intentional?

If not, could the wallet connection logic use the currently selected Aave market / current wallet chain when initializing the Core connection, so Avalanche users can connect directly on chain ID 43114?

governance_posts.title: [Recovery Request] Accidental Direct USDT Transfer to Aave Contract on Celo — rescueTokens Assistance Needed
governance_posts.description:
[Recovery Request] Accidental Direct USDT Transfer to Aave Contract on Celo — rescueTokens Assistance Needed

Date of Incident: June 20, 2026 Network: Celo Posted by: Andrew Kim Joseph

Summary

I previously submitted this request via email to wecare@aave.com and am following up here to ensure visibility with the broader community and relevant stakeholders.

While attempting to supply USDT to Aave on the Celo network, I mistakenly performed a direct ERC-20 token transfer to an Aave-related contract address instead of calling the appropriate supply or supplyWithPermit function. As a result, the tokens were sent directly to the contract without minting the corresponding aTokens, and the funds are now effectively locked.

I am reaching out to the Aave community and governance to inquire whether recovery is possible via the rescueTokens function, and to request that this be reviewed by the relevant parties.

Transaction Details

Field Value
Transaction Hash 0xc26b32a3bb84a8b1672337596fe7cb2906857e70426f4e494e83f07b4406e6ce
Network Celo
Token USDT
Amount 52 USDT
Sender Address 0xbA34711e2F23cCdb893FF2166f7A71f200E76b80
Destination Address 0x3E59A31363E2ad014dcbc521c4a0d5757d9f3402

What Happened

The transfer was made during an attempt to interact with the Aave protocol on Celo. Instead of invoking the supply or supplyWithPermit function on the Pool contract, a raw ERC-20 transfer was executed directly to the contract address. This resulted in the USDT arriving at the contract without triggering the deposit logic, and no aTokens were minted in return.

Recovery Request

I understand that recovery of mistakenly transferred tokens is not always possible and is subject to governance processes. However, given that:

  • The transfer occurred in the context of a direct Aave protocol interaction
  • The destination is an Aave-related contract that may hold recoverable token balances
  • The rescueTokens function exists in Aave contracts for situations such as this

I am kindly requesting that the Aave team or governance review this transaction and advise on whether a rescueTokens call is feasible and appropriate.

Additional Information

I am the owner of the sending address (0xbA34711e2F23cCdb893FF2166f7A71f200E76b80) and am happy to provide any additional verification or information required to assist with the investigation.

Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to any guidance the community or Aave team can offer.

— Andrew Kim Joseph andrewkimjoseph@gmail.com

governance_posts.title: [Risk Stewards] November 2026 - Stablecoin Interest Rate Adjustments
governance_posts.description:
title: [Risk Stewards] November 2026 - Stablecoin Interest Rate Adjustments

author: @TokenLogic

created: 2026-11-17

Overview

TokenLogic proposes updates to stablecoin interest rate parameters across Aave V3 and V4, covering 17 reserves. The proposal increases Slope 1 on 16 reserves, reduces it on Base EURC, and raises Base USDC’s UOptimal from 90% to 92%.

The adjustments reflect differences in borrowing demand, supply dynamics, and borrower composition across markets. Higher rates aim to moderate borrowing demand where utilization is elevated, improve supplier incentives in supply constrained markets, and preserve the profitability of carry trades.

Market structure

Borrowers respond differently to increases in the rate at the kink depending on their strategy. Those borrowing stables against ETH or BTC primarily pay for leverage or liquidity. In contrast, borrowers looping USDe, sUSDe, or Maple syrup tokens rely on the spread between collateral yield and borrowing costs, making the kink rate a key determinant of position profitability.

The stablecoin reserves covered by this proposal account for approximately $3.9B in outstanding debt, but borrower composition varies significantly across markets. Ethereum Core is dominated by blue chip collateral borrowers, while several smaller markets consist primarily of looping positions. This section examines each reserve’s borrower composition, proximity to the kink, and supplier and borrower concentration to inform the reserve specific IRM recommendations that follow.

Collateral behind the debt

Across the reserves in scope, approximately 53% of debt is backed by blue chip collateral, while 39% is attributable to loops involving yield bearing stablecoins. The remainder consists of other or mixed collateral.

Most reserves fall into two distinct groups. Blue chip dominated reserves, such as Ethereum Core USDC and Base USDC, are primarily driven by borrowing against ETH and BTC. Borrowers in these markets are therefore more sensitive to Aave’s competitiveness relative to other lending protocols accepting similar collateral.

In contrast, loop dominated reserves, such as Plasma USDT0 and Mantle USDT0, primarily support carry trades involving yield bearing stablecoins. Demand in these markets depends on the spread between collateral yield and Aave’s borrowing rate, making borrowers more sensitive to changes in the rate at the kink.

Utilization profiles

The chart below shows daily average utilization over the last 60 days against each reserve’s optimal utilization.

Several reserves have remained above the kink for a substantial portion of the observation period. Avalanche USDC spent 54 of 60 days above its 90% kink, with average utilization of 92.1%. Base USDC and Optimism USDC also spent 43 and 41 days above their respective 90% kinks. Ethereum Core USDC averaged 93.8% utilization against a 94% kink, spending 33 days above it.

Elevated utilization has also kept UOptimal on Ethereum Core USDC at 94%.

This sustained utilization may reflect strong borrowing demand, but it can also result from declining supply or borrowers not unwinding positions as borrowing costs increase. The following sections examine these dynamics in more detail.

Base EURC is the exception. Utilization averaged approximately 50% over the period and did not reach the 90% kink on any day. The proposed reduction in Slope 1 aims to make borrowing more attractive and improve utilization of the available liquidity.

Concentration

Concentration indicates how strongly individual participants can influence reserve utilization through supply withdrawals or changes in borrowing positions. The chart below shows the share of total supply and debt held by the largest and ten largest wallets in each reserve.

The largest reserve, Ethereum Core USDC, generally has a distributed borrower base. Ethereum Core USDC has recently seen a $676M inflow from a single wallet on 6 November, bringing its share of total supply to 23.9%.

Loop dominated reserves exhibit substantially higher concentration on both sides. Ethena’s backing wallet accounts for 61.6% of supply in Plasma USDT0 and 74.0% in Mantle USDT0. Borrowing is similarly concentrated, with the ten largest borrowers accounting for 96.0% of debt in Plasma USDT0, 94.3% in Mantle USDT0, and 94.2% in Monad USDC. These markets therefore depend heavily on a limited number of suppliers and borrowers, making utilization particularly sensitive to changes in their positions.

Base USDC presents a more mature reserve profile. The largest supplier holds 3.6% of supply, while the ten largest account for 16.3%. Concentration has declined steadily since listing, with the largest supplier’s share falling from 34% in mid 2024 to 12.5% at the start of 2025. Borrowing is similarly distributed, with the largest borrower accounting for just 4.8% of outstanding debt.

The reserve’s maturity and increasingly broad distribution provide a stronger foundation for operating at higher utilization levels. This makes Base USDC a suitable candidate for a higher UOptimal, particularly given the limited exposure to individual supplier and borrower decisions.

Demand and supply

High utilization can reflect either growing borrowing demand or declining supply while borrowers maintain their positions. These dynamics have different implications for rate adjustments: higher borrowing costs can moderate new demand, while also improving supplier returns and encouraging liquidity.

Reserves at the kink with growing demand

In Ethereum Core USDC and Base USDC, supply grew broadly in line with debt, keeping utilization close to the kink. Ethereum Core USDC growth was largely driven by two wallets on 6 November, including a $676M supply inflow and a $353M USDe backed borrowing position.

Base USDC, in contrast, recorded broader growth, with debt increasing by $14M across a supplier base of thousands of wallets.

Monad USDT0, V4 Core USDT, and V4 Avalanche Core USDC experienced faster debt growth relative to supply. In these reserves, borrowing demand is absorbing available liquidity, making the rate at the kink an important lever for managing further growth.

V4 Plus USDT also recorded strong growth, although from a relatively small base, with supply broadly keeping pace with debt. It is loop dominated, with demand driven by USDe carry trades, examined further in the Carry Trades section.

Supply-constrained reserves

The remaining reserves recorded flat or declining debt. However, utilization remained at or near the kink as supply contracted alongside or faster than debt. Two distinct patterns emerge.

In several reserves, supply withdrawals outpaced debt reductions, pushing utilization higher or keeping it above the kink. Avalanche USDt is the clearest example: supply declined by approximately 13% while debt was unchanged, lifting utilization from 79% to 91%, above its 90% kink. Optimism USDC and V4 Core frxUSD show the same pattern on a smaller scale. This suggests borrowers are maintaining their positions while suppliers withdraw liquidity. In these cases, the rate at the kink primarily influences supplier incentives by improving returns to retain and attract liquidity.

A second group experienced broadly proportional declines in both debt and supply. This pattern is particularly evident in loop dominated reserves such as Monad USDC and Plasma USDT0, where debt and supply declined by approximately 33% and 31%, and 16% and 16%, respectively. This is consistent with loop positions unwinding on both sides, as borrowers repay stablecoins and withdraw their collateral. Utilization in Plasma USDT0 and Monad USDC nevertheless remained at the kink.

Across these reserves, high utilization is not necessarily evidence of growing borrowing demand. Supplier retention and the pace of position unwinding are equally important considerations. For loop dominated markets, maintaining an attractive carry spread also remains relevant, as discussed in the following section.

Carry Trades

Loop dominated reserves are primarily driven by the spread between collateral yield and borrowing costs. This section examines the collateral composition of these reserves, the yields generated by underlying assets and additional incentives, and the resulting returns at the rate at the kink.

USDe is the primary loop collateral across most markets, accounting for 78% of debt in Plasma USDT0, 57% to 59% in Monad USDC and USDT0, 59% in V4 Core frxUSD, nearly all debt in V4 Plus USDT, and 77% in V4 Plus USDC. sUSDe is the main collateral in Mantle USDT0 (52%) and Ethereum USDtb (43%), and accounts for the remaining 23% in V4 Plus USDC.

Maple syrup tokens account for most of the remainder: syrupUSDC in the Monad reserves (24–29%) and syrupUSDT in Mantle USDT0 (30%).

USDe yields are primarily determined by Ethena’s Merkl campaigns, which target a total APR inclusive of Aave’s supply rate. The effective yield depends on whether each campaign’s budget is sufficient to cover the USDe supplied in these markets.

These targets have increased over the past two months and currently stand at 5.25% for V3 markets and 5.75% for V4 Ethereum. Maple syrup tokens accrue yield through their vault exchange rates, generating approximately 5.0% for syrupUSDC and 4.8% for syrupUSDT on average over the past two weeks.

Several markets offer additional incentives on top of these base yields. On Monad, USDe and syrupUSDC suppliers receive additional WMON rewards. These rewards accrue to looping positions.

At maximum leverage, the resulting yield spreads translate into double digit returns on equity across most markets, even at the proposed kink rates. Returns vary across collateral types and markets, ranging from low to high double digits, with USDe loops on V4 and Monad markets generally offering higher returns. The main exception is sUSDe on Plasma USDT0, where returns remain in the single digits due to the relatively narrow spread between collateral yield and borrowing costs. sUSDe accounts for 17% of debt in this reserve.

The proposed rate increases leave most carry strategies attractive, reducing maximum leverage returns by approximately 0.9 to 1.8 percentage points across most markets. V4 Core frxUSD is a notable exception: as the cheapest and most profitable USDe loop market, it receives a larger 50 basis point increase, resulting in a more substantial reduction in returns, although they remain attractive.

Blue-chip reserves

For blue chip dominated reserves, borrowers can generally access similar leverage through other lending protocols accepting ETH and BTC collateral. Aave’s borrowing rates should therefore be evaluated against these alternatives. The chart below compares Aave’s borrow rates with other venues.

On USDC, Aave remains competitively positioned. Ethereum Core USDC averaged 5.14% over the past 30 days, compared with 5.31% on Morpho and 4.58% on SparkLend. SparkLend rates have since increased to approximately 4.9% following its 7 November update, leaving the proposed 4.70% kink below both alternatives. On Base USDC, Aave averaged 6.18% against 5.66% on Morpho, with both trading above the proposed 5.00% kink since October.

On USDT, Aave already prices above comparable alternatives. Over the past 30 days, Ethereum Core USDT and V4 Core USDT averaged 4.98% and 5.34%, respectively, compared with approximately 4.5% on both SparkLend and Morpho. Ethereum Core USDT has also seen supply return in recent days, bringing utilization back below its 94% kink. We therefore leave its Slope 1 unchanged. V4 Core USDT, where debt continues to grow, remains in scope.

Comparable markets are limited for the remaining blue chip reserves. Avalanche USDC and USDt, Optimism USDC, V4 Avalanche Core USDC, and PYUSD borrowers have a cheaper alternative on Morpho, but debt has held through rate spikes. Recommendations for these reserves therefore rely more heavily on the utilization, supply, and concentration dynamics discussed in the previous sections.

governance_posts.description:
title: [Direct-to-AIP] Asset Listing - USDC Plasma
author: @TokenLogic
created: 2026-11-18

Summary

This proposal seeks to onboard native USDC as a supported asset on the Aave V3 Plasma Instance.

Circle deployed USDC natively on Plasma on August 28, 2026, alongside EURC, the Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol, and Bridge Kit. This proposal expands the stablecoin offering on Aave V3 Plasma and gives users an additional highly liquid, fiat-backed asset for supplying, borrowing, and collateral use, configured in line with USDT0.

Motivation

On August 28, 2026, Circle announced native USDC on Plasma, along with institutional on and off ramps through Circle Mint. Circle issues native USDC on Plasma, fully reserved and redeemable 1:1 for US dollars through eligible Circle channels. CCTP enables native USDC to be transferred between Plasma and other supported networks without relying on wrapped or third-party bridged representations.

Aave V3 Plasma is today a USDT0-centric market. USDT0 is the only fiat-backed stablecoin listed and carries roughly $603M of supply against $552M of borrows (about 92% utilisation), with USDe and GHO as the other borrowable stablecoins. Every stablecoin-borrowing eMode category on the instance points to USDT0.

Onboarding USDC to Aave V3 Plasma would:

  • Add a second fiat-backed stablecoin to the instance, reducing single-issuer concentration on the stablecoin side of the book.
  • Provide an additional asset for lending and borrowing alongside USDT0, USDe, and GHO.
  • Increase the stablecoin borrowing liquidity available to the existing USDe, sUSDe, weETH, syrupUSDT, WXPL, GHO and PT-sUSDe eMode categories.
  • Enable users and institutions to access native USDC liquidity supported by Circle Mint and CCTP infrastructure, and to move USDC between Plasma and other Aave deployments (Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Avalanche, X Layer) via CCTP.

Plasma is a stablecoin-focused network, and the arrival of Circle’s native issuance gives Aave V3 Plasma direct access to the second largest stablecoin without bridge dependencies.

Specification

USDC Contract Address

Asset Address
USDC 0x2d661C89D812261039AF9764eceaAee884f5F67F

The address above represents Circle-issued native USDC on Plasma (6 decimals), as published in Circle’s contract address reference.

Proposed Market Configuration

We propose configuring USDC in line with the parameters currently applied to USDT0 on Aave V3 Plasma, consistent with the approach LlamaRisk recommended for the recent USDC listing on X Layer (USDC aligned to the local USDT0 risk parameters, 75% LTV and 78% LT, with a CAPO stable adapter). Supply and borrow caps mirror the X Layer listing and can be raised through the Risk Steward as USDC liquidity on Plasma develops. Final parameters remain subject to Risk Service Provider recommendations.

Final onboarding parameters remain subject to review and recommendations from Aave’s Risk Service Providers.

Liquidity

Native USDC on Plasma is only days old: roughly 4.5M USDC has been minted at the time of writing, and on-chain DEX liquidity is still nascent. As with the X Layer listing, liquidity is expected to build as supply flows to the chain through CCTP and Circle Mint, and the proposed caps leave room for Risk Service Providers to sequence activation or adjust caps based on observed liquidity at execution.

eMode Configuration

We propose adding USDC as a borrowable asset to the eight current-generation eMode categories on Plasma in which USDT0 is borrowable today. This proposal does not modify the collateral, LTV, LT, or Liquidation Bonus parameters for any category; it only adds USDC as a borrowable asset to each mentioned eMode.

Oracle

A Chainlink USDC/USD Price Feed is already available on Plasma Mainnet.

Chainlink identifies this feed as USDC/USD-RefPrice-DF-Plasma-001.

We propose pricing USDC through the Chainlink USDC/USD feed wrapped in a CAPO stable adapter (PriceCapAdapterStable) with the upward price deviation capped at 4% ($1.04), in line with LlamaRisk’s recommendation for USDC on X Layer and identical to the cap of the Capped USDT/USD adapter (0xdBbB0b5DD13E7AC9C56624834ef193df87b022c3) currently used for USDT0 on Plasma. The final oracle configuration is to be confirmed by the relevant Aave Risk and Technical Service Providers.

Disclaimer

TokenLogic is an active service provider to the Aave DAO, the beneficiary of stream 100086 and the KPI as outlined in this publication. The scope of this engagement is available via this forum proposal.

TokenLogic supports and maintains an independent delegate voting platform within the Aave community.

TokenLogic and associated entities have no undisclosed material conflicts of interest at the time of submission.

Next Steps

  1. Gather feedback from the community.
  2. Using the Direct-to-AIP process, incorporate feedback from the Risk Service Provider.
  3. Escalate this proposal to the AIP Voting stage.

We propose configuring USDC in line with the parameters currently applied to USDT0 on Aave V3 Plasma, consistent with the approach LlamaRisk recommended for the recent USDC listing on X Layer (USDC aligned to the local USDT0 risk parameters, 75% LTV and 78% LT, with a CAPO stable adapter). Supply and borrow caps mirror the X Layer listing and can be raised through the Risk Steward as USDC liquidity on Plasma develops. Final parameters remain subject to Risk Service Provider recommendations.

Final onboarding parameters remain subject to review and recommendations from Aave’s Risk Service Providers.

Liquidity

Native USDC on Plasma is only days old: roughly 4.5M USDC has been minted at the time of writing, and on-chain DEX liquidity is still nascent. As with the X Layer listing, liquidity is expected to build as supply flows to the chain through CCTP and Circle Mint, and the proposed caps leave room for Risk Service Providers to sequence activation or adjust caps based on observed liquidity at execution.

eMode Configuration

We propose adding USDC as a borrowable asset to the eight current-generation eMode categories on Plasma in which USDT0 is borrowable today. This proposal does not modify the collateral, LTV, LT, or Liquidation Bonus parameters for any category; it only adds USDC as a borrowable asset to each mentioned eMode.

Oracle

A Chainlink USDC/USD Price Feed is already available on Plasma Mainnet.

Chainlink identifies this feed as USDC/USD-RefPrice-DF-Plasma-001.

We propose pricing USDC through the Chainlink USDC/USD feed wrapped in a CAPO stable adapter (PriceCapAdapterStable) with the upward price deviation capped at 4% ($1.04), in line with LlamaRisk’s recommendation for USDC on X Layer and identical to the cap of the Capped USDT/USD adapter (0xdBbB0b5DD13E7AC9C56624834ef193df87b022c3) currently used for USDT0 on Plasma. The final oracle configuration is to be confirmed by the relevant Aave Risk and Technical Service Providers.

Disclaimer

TokenLogic is an active service provider to the Aave DAO, the beneficiary of stream 100086 and the KPI as outlined in this publication. The scope of this engagement is available via this forum proposal.

TokenLogic supports and maintains an independent delegate voting platform within the Aave community.

TokenLogic and associated entities have no undisclosed material conflicts of interest at the time of submission.

Next Steps

  1. Gather feedback from the community.
  2. Using the Direct-to-AIP process, incorporate feedback from the Risk Service Provider.
  3. Escalate this proposal to the AIP Voting stage.
